title: Where electrons conduct and where to change it: gauge-invariant sensitivities and the networks of sensitive bonds
summary: Where is the electrical current carried in a disordered solid, and where would a local change alter it? The two questions differ. We answer the second exactly: the derivative of the Kubo-Greenwood conductivity with respect to the Hamiltonian is gauge invariant and gives the response to any local change. The construction applies to any Hamiltonian. We try it on amorphous silicon, with tight-binding cells of up to 10000 atoms and density-functional cells of up to 512 atoms, and compare it with three ways of allocating the conductivity: the space-projected conductivity (SPC), KuboMap, and the local density of states (LDOS). KuboMap follows the LDOS closely (median Spearman correlation 0.97). The sensitivity does not. It ranks the response to an on-site shift accurately and the response to removing an atom poorly, and it transfers between Hamiltonians less well than the other maps. The most sensitive bonds form connected clusters. In three large networks they are tree-like filaments of 24 to 38 atoms in the valence tail and looped networks deeper in the gap; the excess over an LDOS-weighted random selection reaches 48 standard deviations and appears only when the broadening spans about five level spacings. The filament overlaps the tail eigenstate with the most weight on it, and one of the leading conduction channels, far more than a random cluster does, but no single state or channel explains it. The networks are largely lost in thermal snapshots at 300 K. Where the conductivity is carried and where it responds are different problems: local transport maps are useful for the first and limited for the second.

AI.tldr: The derivative of the Kubo-Greenwood conductivity with respect to the Hamiltonian is shown to be gauge invariant and yields the exact local response to any local perturbation; applied to amorphous silicon, this sensitivity map behaves differently from conductivity-allocation maps (SPC, KuboMap, LDOS), forming connected filamentary clusters that are largely absent in 300 K thermal snapshots.
AI.motivation: Localizing "where current is carried" and "where a local change would alter current" are distinct questions; existing conductivity-allocation schemes (SPC, KuboMap, LDOS) address only the former, and a principled, gauge-invariant measure of the latter is missing.
AI.method: Uses the gauge-invariant derivative of the Kubo-Greenwood conductivity with respect to the Hamiltonian as an exact sensitivity map, applicable to any Hamiltonian. Benchmarks it against space-projected conductivity (SPC), KuboMap, and LDOS on amorphous silicon using tight-binding cells up to 10,000 atoms and DFT cells up to 512 atoms; quantifies ranking accuracy for on-site shifts versus atom removal, transferability across Hamiltonians, cluster geometry, statistical significance versus LDOS-weighted random selection, overlap with tail eigenstates and conduction channels, and stability under 300 K thermal snapshots.
AI.result: KuboMap tracks the LDOS closely (median Spearman 0.97) whereas sensitivity does not. Sensitivity ranks on-site-shift responses accurately but atom-removal responses poorly, and transfers between Hamiltonians less well than other maps. Most sensitive bonds form connected clusters: tree-like filaments of 24–38 atoms in the valence tail and looped networks deeper in the gap, exceeding LDOS-weighted random selection by 48 standard deviations, emerging only when broadening spans ~five level spacings; these filaments overlap the dominant tail eigenstate and a leading conduction channel more than random clusters, though no single state or channel explains them. The networks are largely lost in 300 K snapshots.
AI.conclusion: Where conductivity is carried and where it responds are distinct problems: local transport maps are useful for the former but limited for the latter, and the Hamiltonian-derivative sensitivity provides the exact, gauge-invariant answer to the response question.

title: Three-mode chimera-like states in a minimal network of active camphor ribbons
summary: Chimera states are a remarkable manifestation of symmetry breaking, wherein identical units spontaneously split into coherent and incoherent groups. The term "chimera" itself is inspired by the mythological creature having parts of different animals, reflecting the coexistence of distinct dynamical behaviors within a single system. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the existence of a three-mode chimera-like state in a system of four identical camphor-infused elliptical rotors, each pivoted at a corner of a square base. When placed on a water surface, the rotors self-propel and rotate due to Marangoni-driven flows. Chemical coupling mediated through the shared water interface gives rise to three distinct collective dynamical states, namely a synchronized one, an antisynchronized one and an incoherent one. Our results validate recent theoretical work about three-domain chimeras in reaction-diffusion models, providing new insights into nonlinear dynamics and suggesting that this new type of chimera may be observed in a broad class of physical systems.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of a three-mode chimera-like state among four identical camphor-infused elliptical rotors coupled via Marangoni-driven flows on a shared water surface.
AI.motivation: Chimera states—spontaneous symmetry breaking where identical units split into coherent and incoherent groups—are striking but challenging to realize experimentally; the authors seek to demonstrate a three-domain (three-mode) chimera-like state predicted theoretically for reaction-diffusion models.
AI.method: Four identical camphor-infused elliptical rotors are pivoted at the corners of a square base on a water surface. They self-propel and rotate via Marangoni-driven flows, and are chemically coupled through the shared water interface, yielding three collective dynamical states: synchronized, antisynchronized, and incoherent.
AI.result: Three distinct collective dynamical states are observed: a synchronized mode, an antisynchronized mode, and an incoherent mode, constituting a three-mode chimera-like state.
AI.conclusion: The experiment validates recent theoretical work on three-domain chimeras in reaction-diffusion models, offers new insights into nonlinear dynamics, and suggests this new type of chimera may be observable in a broad class of physical systems.

title: Onset of subdiffusion in dephased quasiperiodic lattices
summary: Dephasing is widely expected to induce diffusion in quasiperiodic lattices due to the loss of phase coherence. However, this expectation can fail dramatically in lattices possessing singular onsite potentials or vanishing hoppings which are expected to trivially localize the particle. Remarkably, we show that the transport in such lattices can be subdiffusive under proper conditions for which the "mean resistance" of the lattice diverges. As a result, we obtain a transition from diffusive to subdiffusive transport depending on the strength of quasiperiodic modulation. Even more strikingly, the transport is slowest not deep in the subdiffusive regime but precisely at its onset, forming a sharp "subdiffusive trench". Our analytical and numerical analysis reveal that the transport exponents are universal, fixed solely by the order of singularities (zeros) of the diagonal (off-diagonal) quasiperiodic modulation. In the end, we complement our findings through exact Lindblad simulations and provide possible experimental routes to realize such non-trivial transport.

AI.tldr: Dephasing in quasiperiodic lattices with singular onsite potentials or vanishing hoppings can produce subdiffusive (not diffusive) transport when the lattice "mean resistance" diverges, with universal exponents set by the order of the singularities and a sharp "subdiffusive trench" at the diffusion–subdiffusion onset.
AI.motivation: Dephasing is generally thought to induce diffusion in quasiperiodic lattices by destroying phase coherence. The authors challenge this expectation in special lattices with singular diagonal potentials or zero off-diagonal hoppings, which are naively expected to localize particles trivially. They ask whether dephasing can instead generate genuinely non-trivial, subdiffusive transport and what controls its character.
AI.method: Analytical treatment based on the "mean resistance" of the lattice as a diagnostic for transport, combined with numerical simulations of the dephasing dynamics. Exact Lindblad master-equation simulations validate the results, and the authors identify experimental routes for realizing such transport.
AI.result: Transport becomes subdiffusive under conditions where the lattice mean resistance diverges, giving a diffusive-to-subdiffusive transition tuned by the strength of the quasiperiodic modulation. The slowest transport occurs not deep in the subdiffusive regime but precisely at its onset, forming a sharp "subdiffusive trench." Transport exponents are universal, determined solely by the order of the singularities (zeros) of the diagonal (off-diagonal) quasiperiodic modulation.
AI.conclusion: Dephasing-induced transport in quasiperiodic lattices with singular potentials or vanishing hoppings is richer than the standard diffusion picture: it can be subdiffusive with universal, singularity-order-determined exponents and a non-monotonic slowdown at the transition. Lindblad simulations support the predictions, and the effect is proposed as experimentally accessible.

title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation
summary: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes adding an optimization loop to Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) that learns the Hamiltonian evolution time to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured phase distributions, thereby overcoming phase digitization error and improving minimum-eigenvalue accuracy without increasing phase-qubit count.
AI.motivation: Standard QPE accuracy is fundamentally bounded by phase digitization error tied to the number of phase qubits, demanding deep circuits that are impractical on near-term hardware. The authors seek a way to improve analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase without adding qubits.
AI.method: An optimization loop learns the Hamiltonian evolution time parameter of the QPE circuit so as to minimize the Shannon entropy of the measured eigenvalue (phase) distribution. This exploits the natural correspondence between phase-distribution entropy and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase, introducing parameter learning into QPE.
AI.result: Numerical demonstrations on quantum magnet models show that entropy-minimizing evolution-time learning substantially improves minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy, enabling shorter-depth QPE circuits.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-based evolution-time learning circumvents phase digitization limits, makes QPE more feasible for near-term fundamental science applications, and introduces a new paradigm of parameter learning within QPE.

title: Entanglement Geometry Beyond Polygons: Graph-Theoretic Entanglement Inequalities
summary: Entanglement entropies of pure multipartite states can be constrained by organizing subsystem cuts as edges (hyperedges) of graphs (hypergraphs). Starting from the one-party entanglement polygon inequality, we derive these constraints from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity, with optimal coefficients and explicit equality conditions. Our central result determines, for a distinguished two-party cut and an arbitrary weighted family of cuts, the optimal polygon coefficient: the smallest total weight of the cuts separating a member of the distinguished pair from a remaining party. A refinement involving three mutual information terms gives the exact minimum of the weighted sum at fixed entropies of the two parties and of their union, attained by at most three independent bipartite pure states. This criterion recovers the cycle and complete-graph inequalities and shows that uniform incidence parity, which we prove sufficient for polygon inequalities on hypergraphs, is not necessary. Averaging strong subadditivity over both sides of a bipartition gives a sharp $k$-marginal inequality with coefficient $2\binom{n-2}{k-1}$, and we determine uniformly optimal coefficients for collective hyperstar inequalities. For paths and overlapping hyperchains, the deficits are exact sums of conditional mutual information terms; genuinely multipartite entangled cluster states saturate the hyperchain inequality while the chain inequality remains strict. We characterize pure chain equality states, bound the trace distance to cycle equality states independently of the number of parties and local dimensions, and obtain bond-dimension bounds for matrix product states and sequential-recovery error estimates.

AI.tldr: Entanglement entropies of pure multipartite states are constrained by graph/hypergraph-organized cuts. The paper determines optimal polygon coefficients for a distinguished two-party cut over arbitrary weighted cut families, refines the result via three mutual-information terms, and applies it to hypergraphs, k-marginal, hyperstar, path, and hyperchain inequalities with exact equality conditions.
AI.motivation: Entanglement (entropy) inequalities for multipartite pure states are often expressed geometrically as polygon-type constraints on subsystem cuts, but previously known inequalities lacked optimal coefficients, general cut-family scope, and explicit equality conditions. A unified derivation with sharp constants from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity is needed.
AI.method: Model subsystem cuts as edges/hyperedges of graphs/hypergraphs. Derive constraints from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity, starting from the one-party entanglement polygon inequality. For a distinguished two-party cut and a weighted family of cuts, compute the optimal polygon coefficient as the smallest total weight of cuts separating a member of the distinguished pair from a remaining party. Add a refinement using three mutual-information terms to obtain the exact weighted-sum minimum at fixed entropies of the two parties and their union, attained by at most three independent bipartite pure states. Average strong subadditivity over both sides of a bipartition; prove incidence-parity sufficiency for hypergraph polygon inequalities; analyze paths, chains, and cluster states; bound trace distance to cycle equality states; derive MPS bond-dimension and sequential-recovery error bounds.
AI.result: The optimal polygon coefficient is characterized exactly, with equality attained by at most three independent bipartite pure states; this recovers cycle and complete-graph inequalities and shows uniform incidence parity is sufficient but not necessary for hypergraph polygon inequalities. Averaging strong subadditivity yields a sharp k-marginal inequality with coefficient 2*C(n-2,k-1); uniformly optimal coefficients are found for collective hyperstar inequalities. For paths and overlapping hyperchains, deficits equal exact sums of conditional mutual information terms; genuinely multipartite entangled cluster states saturate the hyperchain inequality while the chain inequality stays strict. Pure chain equality states are characterized; trace distance to cycle equality states is bounded independently of party number and local dimension; MPS bond-dimension bounds and sequential-recovery error estimates follow.
AI.conclusion: Organizing entanglement-entropy constraints via (hyper)graph cuts and averaging strong subadditivity yields optimal-coefficient, tight multipartite entropy inequalities with explicit equality conditions, unifying polygon, cycle, complete-graph, k-marginal, hyperstar, path, and hyperchain inequalities. The results yield structural classifications of equality states and practical consequences for MPS bond dimension and state-recovery accuracy.

title: Tunable Ground-State Entanglement in Fully Connected Quantum Systems: From Logarithmic to Volume-Law Scaling
summary: Entanglement scaling is a central probe of the complexity of quantum many-body ground states, yet once geometric locality is absent, it can depend sensitively on the structure and normalization of interactions. For fully connected Hamiltonians with the natural Kac normalization, nondegenerate gapped ground states are known to obey a logarithmic entanglement bound. Here we ask how the ground-state entanglement changes when this interaction normalization is continuously relaxed away from the Kac scale. We answer this question by constructing an explicit all-to-all bipartite Hamiltonian of $n$ qubits with Fourier pairing amplitudes and pairwise interaction strength proportional to $n^{-κ}$. For sufficiently small fixed coupling, we prove that every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $Θ(n^{2-2κ} \log n)$ for $1/2<κ\leq1$ and $Θ(n)$ at $κ=1/2$. We further show that the ground state is unique and separated from the rest of the spectrum by a system-size-independent gap for $3/4 \leq κ\leq 1$, while weak-coupling analysis and numerical calculations suggest that the gap remains open also for $1/2 \leq κ< 3/4$. Thus, varying only the interaction normalization yields a controlled hierarchy from logarithmic scaling at the natural Kac normalization $κ=1$ to increasingly strong subextensive entanglement and ultimately to a volume law, showing that even an arbitrarily weak relaxation of this normalization precludes a universal logarithmic entanglement bound.

AI.tldr: For an all-to-all bipartite qubit Hamiltonian with interaction strength scaled as $n^{-\kappa}$, every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $\Theta(n^{2-2\kappa}\log n)$ for $1/2<\kappa\leq 1$ and $\Theta(n)$ at $\kappa=1/2$, so even weak relaxation of Kac normalization destroys the universal logarithmic entanglement bound.
AI.motivation: Entanglement scaling probes ground-state complexity, but without geometric locality it depends sensitively on interaction structure and normalization. Fully connected Hamiltonians with natural Kac normalization ($\kappa=1$) are known to obey a logarithmic entanglement bound for nondegenerate gapped ground states. The authors ask how ground-state entanglement changes when the interaction normalization is continuously relaxed away from the Kac scale.
AI.method: Constructs an explicit all-to-all bipartite Hamiltonian of $n$ qubits with Fourier pairing amplitudes and pairwise interaction strength proportional to $n^{-\kappa}$. Uses rigorous proofs at sufficiently small fixed coupling to bound entanglement entropy of every pure ground state, establishes uniqueness of the ground state and a system-size-independent spectral gap for $3/4\leq\kappa\leq 1$, and supplements with weak-coupling analysis and numerics for $1/2\leq\kappa<3/4$.
AI.result: Every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $\Theta(n^{2-2\kappa}\log n)$ for $1/2<\kappa\leq 1$ and $\Theta(n)$ at $\kappa=1/2$. The ground state is unique and separated by a size-independent gap for $3/4\leq\kappa\leq 1$; weak-coupling analysis and numerics suggest the gap stays open for $1/2\leq\kappa<3/4$.
AI.conclusion: Varying only the interaction normalization produces a controlled hierarchy from logarithmic scaling at the natural Kac normalization ($\kappa=1$) to increasingly strong subextensive entanglement and ultimately to a volume law ($\kappa=1/2$), showing that even an arbitrarily weak relaxation of the Kac normalization precludes a universal logarithmic entanglement bound.

title: The Clifford Hierarchy from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D
summary: The Bravyi-König theorem limits the constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to be in the Clifford group. Known qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers exceed it by only one level of the Clifford hierarchy, and this was conjectured to hold generally. We show that this bound can be completely bypassed, and that topological codes with Clifford stabilizers in 2D can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. We present two explicit constructions of codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of $D_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$, with $k$ logical qubits and a logical $C^{k-1}Z$ gate, which is at level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits realizing the gates consist only of physical $Z$ or $CZ$ gates. The main new ingredient comes from the logical encoding, which depends crucially on non-Abelian group multiplication.

AI.tldr: By using non-Abelian topological codes (copies of quantum doubles of D4 and Z2), the authors construct 2D Clifford-stabilizer codes with k logical qubits and a transversal logical C^{k-1}Z gate at level k of the Clifford hierarchy, completely bypassing the Bravyi-König bound.
AI.motivation: The Bravyi-König theorem restricts constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to the Clifford group, and known qubit codes were conjectured to exceed this by at most one level of the Clifford hierarchy. The authors aim to test and overturn this conjectured limitation.
AI.method: Two explicit code constructions are given, based on copies of the quantum doubles of D4 and Z2. The logical encoding crucially relies on non-Abelian group multiplication, and the physical circuits realizing the logical gates use only physical Z or CZ gates.
AI.result: The constructed codes realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy despite having Clifford stabilizers. Specifically, codes with k logical qubits admit a logical C^{k-1}Z gate at level k, implemented by constant-depth physical circuits of Z/CZ gates.
AI.conclusion: The Bravyi-König bound and the one-level conjecture can be completely bypassed; non-Abelian group structure in the logical encoding enables Clifford-stabilizer 2D topological codes to achieve arbitrarily high Clifford-hierarchy logical gates transversally.

title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
summary: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "dynamical averaging," an algorithm that estimates ground-state expectation values in neural-network quantum states by averaging over a real-time-evolved state or observable, achieving up-to-quadratic error suppression that matches the fast convergence of energy without extra energy minimization or increased model complexity.
AI.motivation: In variational energy minimization of neural-network quantum states, energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, but other observables converge only linearly. This disparity limits the accuracy of physical predictions for quantities beyond the energy.
AI.method: Dynamical averaging estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real time. Using insights from quantum information, the authors provide a proof of up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground-state observables, exploiting the effect of randomization on quantum states rather than further optimization or added model capacity.
AI.result: The authors prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground-state observables, matching the convergence rate of the energy. Demonstrated on non-integrable spin models, the method accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical averaging closes the convergence-rate gap in neural-network quantum states, improving observable accuracy to match energy convergence without additional energy minimization or increased model complexity, with validation on non-integrable spin models.

title: Passive memories beyond the Ising model: from SFQ to GKP
summary: Self-correcting quantum memories are spin Hamiltonians that aim to generalize the classical memory of the magnetic hard disk (i.e. ferromagnetic Ising model) to protect against both bit flips and phase flips. Beyond the magnetic hard disk, there are other passive classical memories that are used in modern computers, notably: the flash memory in laptops (which traps charge on a conducting island), and the flux storage loop in single-flux quantum (SFQ) logic (which traps flux in a superconducting loop). In this paper we review how storage and writing work in these two classical memories, drawing analogies to the charge qubit and the flux qubit. Protection in these systems derives not from scaling a lattice to the thermodynamic limit, but from a large, tunable energy barrier that separates codewords during memory, yet can be suppressed during a write. Towards protecting a qubit: We introduce a 2D ``floating XY model'' that combines the exponential (phase-flip) protection of the floating charge island with the polynomial (bit-flip) protection of the ferromagnetic XY model. We also study a self-dual superconducting circuit that hosts GKP codewords as symmetry-broken ground states of a $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 $-symmetric circuit, and discuss its protection and limitations.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews storage/writing in two classical memories (flash charge-trap and SFQ flux loop) and transfers their design principle—protection via a large tunable barrier rather than thermodynamic scaling—to qubits, introducing a 2D floating XY model combining exponential phase-flip and polynomial bit-flip protection, plus a self-dual circuit hosting GKP codewords as symmetry-broken ground states.
AI.motivation: Self-correcting quantum memories seek to generalize the ferromagnetic Ising hard-disk memory to protect against both bit and phase flips, but thermodynamic-limit scaling is impractical; passive classical memories in modern computers (flash, SFQ flux loops) offer an alternative design principle based on large, tunable energy barriers.
AI.method: Review of charge storage/write mechanisms in flash memory and flux storage in SFQ loops, with analogies drawn to charge and flux qubits; construction of a 2D "floating XY model" merging the floating charge island's exponential phase-flip protection with the ferromagnetic XY model's polynomial bit-flip protection; study of a self-dual superconducting circuit whose Z2 x Z2-symmetric ground states are GKP codewords.
AI.result: The floating XY model yields exponential protection against phase flips and polynomial protection against bit flips; the self-dual circuit realizes GKP codewords as symmetry-broken ground states, and its protection mechanisms and limitations are characterized.
AI.conclusion: Barrier-engineering—large and tunable during memory, suppressible during write—offers a viable route to qubit protection without requiring lattice scaling to the thermodynamic limit; the floating XY model and self-dual GKP circuit are concrete proposals in this direction.

title: Birthday-Scale Non-Adaptive Security for Strong Pseudorandom Unitaries
summary:
Pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) are efficiently implementable unitary ensembles that are computationally indistinguishable from Haar-random unitaries, providing efficient substitutes for Haar-randomness in quantum information and cryptography. Strong PRUs require this indistinguishability to hold even when the adversary is given access to all of $U$, $U^\dagger$, $U^*$, and $U^T$.
  In this work, we prove birthday-scale non-adaptive security for the DPFC (Clifford-Phase-Permutation-Clifford) strong PRU candidate. For an $N$-dimensional unitary, allowing arbitrary entangled inputs and coherent superpositions of query types, we show that DPFC can withstand $t \approx \sqrt{N}$ queries. This matches the best known query complexity even for PRUs that are not strong, compared with $t \approx N^α$ for $α< 1/2$ in previous strong-PRU analyses.
  Our proof utilizes two techniques from previous works: the EPR-sector decomposition of Schuster et al. (arXiv 2025), previously used for unitary designs but not for PRUs, and the path-recording framework of Ma and Huang (STOC 2025), previously used for adaptive security analysis.
  We complement the non-adaptive security result with an upper bound in the adaptive setting, showing that DPFC cannot remain secure for $t \gg \sqrt{N}$ queries.

AI.tldr: The authors prove birthday-scale (t ≈ √N) non-adaptive security for the DPFC strong-PRU candidate against adversaries with access to U, U†, U*, U^T, allowing entangled inputs and coherent query superpositions, and show an adaptive upper bound of t ≫ √N.
AI.motivation: Strong pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) must remain indistinguishable from Haar-random unitaries even when the adversary accesses U, U†, U*, and U^T simultaneously, but prior strong-PRU security analyses only reached t ≈ N^α queries for α < 1/2, far below the √N birthday bound known for (even non-strong) PRUs.
AI.method: The proof combines the EPR-sector decomposition of Schuster et al. (arXiv 2025), previously applied to unitary designs, with the path-recording framework of Ma and Huang (STOC 2025), previously used for adaptive security. These are adapted to analyze the DPFC (Clifford-Phase-Permutation-Clifford) construction under arbitrary entangled inputs and coherent superpositions of query types.
AI.result: DPFC withstands t ≈ √N queries in the non-adaptive setting with entangled inputs and coherent query-type superpositions, matching the best known query complexity for non-strong PRUs and improving over the prior t ≈ N^α (α < 1/2) strong-PRU bounds. An adaptive-setting upper bound shows DPFC fails for t ≫ √N.
AI.conclusion: DPFC achieves birthday-bound non-adaptive strong-PRU security, and the adaptive upper bound delimits its security ceiling, narrowing the gap between strong- and non-strong-PRU query complexities while leaving full adaptive security as an open direction.

title: A Basis-Dependent Kernel for Learning Quantum Phases of Matter
summary: Identifying the phases of a quantum many-body system as its parameters vary is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. Data-driven approaches address this task by comparing quantum states, for instance through their fidelity, and locating transitions where these comparisons change abruptly. In this work, we introduce the inverse participation ratio (IPR) kernel, a kernel method built for learning quantum phases of matter from IPRs in physically motivated bases. Unlike fidelity-based kernels, the IPR kernel can identify states with physically meaningful similarity even when they are orthogonal. We test the method on ground states of the transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and Heisenberg XXZ models. For TFIM Gibbs states, we further show that the IPR kernel retains phase-relevant structure over a range of nonzero temperatures where the phase signal of fidelity-based kernels is already degraded. More broadly, our results suggest that quantum kernels benefit more from feature maps tailored to the physics of the problem than from maximal expressivity.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce the "IPR kernel," a quantum kernel method that uses inverse participation ratios (IPRs) in physically motivated bases to learn quantum phases of matter, enabling similarity comparison even between orthogonal states and retaining phase structure at finite temperature.
AI.motivation: Identifying quantum phases as parameters vary is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. Existing data-driven approaches typically compare quantum states via fidelity-based kernels, but these fail to capture physically meaningful similarity when states are orthogonal, and their phase signal degrades at nonzero temperature.
AI.method: The paper proposes a kernel method built on inverse participation ratios (IPRs) computed in physically motivated bases. Rather than comparing states directly through overlap/fidelity, the kernel compares their IPR feature representations, allowing states that are orthogonal to still be recognized as physically similar. The method is tested on ground states of the transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and Heisenberg XXZ models, and on TFIM Gibbs states at finite temperature.
AI.result: The IPR kernel identifies states with physically meaningful similarity even when they are orthogonal. It successfully distinguishes phases in the TFIM and Heisenberg XXZ ground-state problems. For TFIM Gibbs states, the IPR kernel retains phase-relevant structure over a range of nonzero temperatures where fidelity-based kernels' phase signal is already degraded.
AI.conclusion: Quantum kernels benefit more from feature maps tailored to the physics of the problem than from maximal expressivity, and IPR-based feature maps offer a robust alternative to fidelity-based kernels for phase detection.

title: Modeling couplings and quench dynamics of hundred-qubit quantum processors
summary: Quantum processors now operate beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, yet their design and verification rest on precise models of the device. Understanding which properties of quantum processors can still be predicted on classical computers is central both to building these machines and to delimiting claims of quantum advantage. Here we address this question at the device level, using continuous unitary transformations to derive effective Hamiltonians non-perturbatively for two-dimensional superconducting processors at a cost polynomial in qubit number. For a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, we extract the effective qubit couplings, state-dependent interactions (e.g., ZZ couplings), and eigenstate locality that guide processor design. This computation parallelizes over tensor contractions and thus takes an hour at most per design point on a single GPU, enabling rapid design iterations of the full array. Combining these effective models with semiclassical sampling, we then predict the quench dynamics of 100 qubits and 180 couplers at half filling, a sector of dimension $10^{29}$, and validate the approach against exact dynamics of smaller arrays. We show that our approach captures relaxation, thermalization, and transport, but not the bitstring statistics underlying cross-entropy benchmarks. The predicted transport carries a fingerprint of the device: under a staggered detuning, excitations cross over from ballistic to diffusive spreading, slow down at a doublon resonance, and diffuse at different rates on each sublattice. Our results chart which observables lie within classical reach and offer a practical tool for designing future devices.

AI.tldr: Continuous unitary transformations yield non-perturbative effective Hamiltonians for 2D superconducting processors at polynomial cost, enabling GPU-accelerated design and semiclassical prediction of 100-qubit quench dynamics—though not the bitstring statistics behind cross-entropy benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Quantum processors now exceed exact classical simulation, yet their design and verification rely on precise device models. It is therefore central to determine which device properties remain classically predictable, both for building processors and for delimiting quantum-advantage claims.
AI.method: Continuous unitary transformations are used to derive effective Hamiltonians non-perturbatively for 2D superconducting processors, at cost polynomial in qubit number, parallelized over tensor contractions. These effective models are combined with semiclassical sampling to predict quench dynamics.
AI.result: For a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, the method extracts effective qubit couplings, state-dependent ZZ interactions, and eigenstate locality, running in ≤1 hour per design point on a single GPU. Applied at half filling to 100 qubits and 180 couplers (sector dimension 10^29) and validated against exact small-array dynamics, it captures relaxation, thermalization, and transport—but not bitstring statistics. Transport shows a device fingerprint: staggered detuning drives ballistic-to-diffusive crossover, slowing at a doublon resonance and sublattice-dependent diffusion rates.
AI.conclusion: The work maps which observables lie within classical reach and provides a practical, scalable tool for designing future superconducting quantum devices.

title: Certified Discovery of Quantum Phase Diagrams
summary: Can a machine provably discover new quantum phases of matter? We show that the answer is yes under physically motivated assumptions. For any smooth family of geometrically local Hamiltonians, we construct an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs the phase diagram to prescribed accuracy and provides a verifiable certificate for every transition it reports. The algorithm takes as input only a classical description of the family together with unverified preparations of reference ground states; no order parameter, symmetry-breaking pattern, or training data are supplied. It succeeds provided that at least one preparation is correct in each gapped region of parameter space. The algorithm explores parameter space by quasi-adiabatically or adiabatically transporting each reference state, detecting the approach of a phase boundary by tapping the transported state with a frequency-filtered local probe: excitations created by the probe witness the closing of the energy gap. We prove that the gap closing for continuous phase transitions can always be detected using the frequency-filtered gradient of the Hamiltonian. The gap-detecting measurement is gentle, so when the ground state is unique a single reusable copy of each reference ground state supports the full exploration (for degenerate ground states, polynomially many copies suffice). The quantum algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution. We also give a classical algorithm that runs in quasipolynomial time at constant gap resolution. Numerical experiments demonstrate how our algorithm accurately determines the phase structure of several model quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that a machine can provably discover new quantum phases of matter: given only classical descriptions of geometrically local Hamiltonian families plus unverified reference ground states, an efficient quantum algorithm outputs the phase diagram to prescribed accuracy and certifies every reported transition.
AI.motivation: Existing machine-learning approaches to phase discovery rely on training data, assumed order parameters, or symmetry-breaking patterns, and lack rigorous guarantees. The authors ask whether a machine can provably (with certificates) discover phases and transitions under physically motivated assumptions.
AI.method: For any smooth family of geometrically local Hamiltonians, the algorithm takes a classical description plus unverified preparations of reference ground states (at least one correct per gapped region). It quasi-adiabatically or adiabatically transports each reference state through parameter space, detecting incipient phase boundaries via a frequency-filtered local probe: probe-induced excitations witness gap closing. It is proven that gap closing for continuous transitions is always detectable using the frequency-filtered gradient of the Hamiltonian. The measurement is gentle, so one reusable copy suffices for unique ground states (polynomially many for degenerate ones). A classical variant runs in quasipolynomial time at constant gap resolution.
AI.result: The quantum algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution and outputs the phase diagram with a verifiable certificate for each transition, using no order parameter, symmetry-breaking pattern, or training data. Numerical experiments show it accurately determines the phase structure of several model quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: Under physically motivated assumptions, machine discovery of quantum phases is provably possible, with efficient quantum and quasipolynomial classical algorithms providing certified phase diagrams; this establishes rigorous foundations for automated, certificate-backed phase discovery.

title: Self-testing in Fermionic Networks
comment: 6 pages main text, 2 pages end matter, 37 pages Supplemental Material. Comments welcome
summary: Self-testing certifies quantum states and measurements from observed correlations alone, without assumptions on the inner workings of the devices. Its standard formulation, however, models the devices as manipulating qudits, of arbitrary or even infinite dimension. Yet febits, information encoded in the presence or absence of a fermion in a mode, can produce correlations in quantum networks that no qudit model reproduces under the same locality constraints. We first show that the modeling choice in terms of qudits or febits matters for self-testing: some correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy admit two fermionic realizations inequivalent under local parity-preserving isometries. We then develop a fermionic self-testing framework and show that the correlations of a three-party rewiring network single out febit states and measurements up to such isometries, providing the first genuine fermionic self-test.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using qudits vs. febits (fermionic occupation modes) as the device model changes self-testing conclusions, and presents the first genuine fermionic self-test by showing a three-party rewiring network's correlations uniquely certify febit states and measurements up to local parity-preserving isometries.
AI.motivation: Standard self-testing models devices as manipulating qudits of arbitrary or infinite dimension, but fermionic encodings (febits—information in presence/absence of a fermion in a mode) can generate quantum-network correlations that no qudit model reproduces under the same locality constraints. It is therefore unclear whether the qudit assumption is innocuous for self-testing, motivating a fermionic treatment.
AI.method: The authors first demonstrate the model-dependence by exhibiting correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy yet admit two fermionic realizations inequivalent under local parity-preserving isometries. They then construct a fermionic self-testing framework and analyze the correlations of a three-party rewiring network within it.
AI.result: The modeling choice (qudit vs. febit) provably matters: some uniquely-qudit-self-tested correlations have two inequivalent fermionic realizations. Within the new framework, the three-party rewiring network's correlations single out febit states and measurements up to local parity-preserving isometries.
AI.conclusion: Self-testing must be formulated relative to the physical encoding (fermionic vs. qudit). The work establishes the first genuine fermionic self-test, certifying febit states and measurements from correlations alone.

title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
summary: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

AI.tldr: A measurement-free, gate-based QEC protocol is adapted from photonics to a cQED architecture with three coupled microwave cavities, correcting single-photon loss with 99% fidelity and extending logical lifetime 1.2–1.8× beyond the unprotected Fock encoding.
AI.motivation: Large-scale quantum computation requires QEC, but QEC overhead is demanding. Correcting dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing residual errors to an outer code reduces these demands. Prior work (Krastanov et al.) proposed a measurement-free, coherent-control photonic protocol for photon loss; this paper aims to realize such an approach in a superconducting cQED platform.
AI.method: Logical qubit encoded in the lowest-order binomial code of one superconducting microwave cavity; two additional cavities serve as ancillas; the three cavities are coupled via Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. The protocol is measurement-free and gate-based, evaluated through numerical simulations using experimentally realistic parameters, including optimization of the waiting time between successive error-correction rounds.
AI.result: Single-photon loss is corrected with 99% fidelity. Optimized inter-round waiting time extends logical lifetime by a factor of 1.2–1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock {|0⟩, |1⟩} encoding, surpassing break-even performance.
AI.conclusion: Gate-based, measurement-free QEC in cQED is experimentally feasible with realistic parameters and demonstrates break-even operation, highlighting its potential for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
summary: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD similarity (1-TVD). On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a translator that converts quantum circuits from multiple MLIR dialects into QIR by choosing among a deterministic compiler path for known grammars, an LLM agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path triggered on test failure, validated by a dual-backend simulator pipeline comparing output distributions via total variation distance.
AI.motivation: Each quantum framework defines its own MLIR dialect, so porting a circuit to a QIR runtime currently requires a hand-written conversion pass per dialect, which does not scale across diverse frontends.
AI.method: A three-path translator: (1) deterministic compilation for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), (2) an LLM agentic path for unseen dialects, and (3) a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators and compares output distributions by TVD. For smaller open-weight models, retrieval-augmented generation is replaced by inline context engineering, plus a guardrail assembler that reconstructs valid QIR from incomplete output.
AI.result: Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD similarity (1-TVD). On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.
AI.conclusion: Combining deterministic compilation, LLM-driven agentic translation, and repair, together with simulator-based TVD validation, yields a robust and generalizable dialect-to-QIR translation framework that remains exact on known grammars and delivers first-iteration success on unseen dialects.

title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs.
  We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.

AI.tldr: Introduces Block Checks, a unified check construction, and a Pareto tree search that jointly explores check design and auxiliary-block sharing to generate post-selection circuits with improved operation–depth trade-offs for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires logical states prepared so single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection detects dangerous faults via added checks and discards the run, but the measurement scheme determines circuit depth and operation count, and the optimal trade-off is hardware-dependent. Existing automated methods each fix one check construction, yielding a single fixed trade-off rather than a tunable design space.
AI.method: Block Checks: several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which subsumes existing constructions and places them in a single design space. A Pareto tree search then explores this space by adding checks and auxiliary blocks, merging auxiliaries, and editing the circuit, optimizing operation–depth trade-offs on a Pareto front.
AI.result: On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation–depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source in the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT qecc), and circuits are available in the QECirc library.
AI.conclusion: Unifying check constructions under Block Checks and searching the combined space yields superior, Pareto-optimal post-selection circuits across multiple operation–depth trade-offs, providing hardware-adaptive fault-tolerant state preparation beyond fixed-construction baselines.

title: A Quantum Continuous Wavelet Transform
summary: We construct a quantum continuous wavelet transform (QCWT) on a finite scale--translation grid whose scales may be non-dyadic. A quantum Fourier transform places the amplitude-encoded signal in the frequency basis, the scale-dependent multiplier is block-encoded with one flag qubit, and an inverse Fourier transform returns the complex, quadrature-weighted CWT coefficients in the success branch. For heralded circuits that act once on one copy of the input with an input-independent output factor, we bound the success probability and attain the bound by a frequency-conditioned scale preparation. When the scale prior is prepared independently of frequency, normalizing the multiplier separately at each scale is optimal and raises the success probability by factors of 4.9 and 14.6 in our examples; on logarithmic grids this architecture loses, relative to the bound, a factor of about the admissibility constant over the squared spectral peak times the logarithmic scale range. We give a fixed-point resource estimate for a reversible Mexican-hat multiplier, the multinomial law of scale--translation measurements, and Hadamard tests for complex coefficients. We show that a Fourier-basis measurement of the input, followed by classical randomization, reproduces the flag and scale outcomes of every such heralded circuit exactly, so it is at least as informative for global scale energies; a simulation study of Hurst exponent estimation agrees. What the QCWT adds is the joint scale--translation law: two chirps with identical Fourier-basis and time-basis measurement laws have QCWT laws at total-variation distance 0.27.

AI.tldr: A heralded quantum continuous wavelet transform on finite scale–translation grids with non-dyadic scales is constructed, its success probability is bounded and attained, and it is shown that a classical Fourier-basis measurement reproduces all its flag/scale outcomes exactly, while the QCWT's added value is a rich joint scale–translation law.
AI.motivation: Wavelet analysis is central to multiscale signal processing, but quantum analogues have largely been restricted to dyadic scales and lack a rigorous account of success probability, normalization, and resource cost. The paper aims to define a QCWT on general (non-dyadic) finite scale–translation grids and to clarify what quantum information processing genuinely adds over simpler measurement strategies.
AI.method: The signal is amplitude encoded and mapped to the frequency basis via a quantum Fourier transform; a scale-dependent multiplier is block-encoded controlled by one flag qubit, and an inverse Fourier transform returns quadrature-weighted complex CWT coefficients in the success branch. For heralded circuits acting once on one copy with an input-independent output factor, a success-probability bound is derived and attained through a frequency-conditioned scale preparation. The authors analyze frequency-independent scale priors (per-scale multiplier normalization), quantify the loss on logarithmic grids via the admissibility constant, and give a fixed-point resource estimate for a reversible Mexican-hat multiplier, the multinomial law of scale–translation measurements, and Hadamard tests for complex coefficients.
AI.result: The success-probability bound is attained; per-scale normalization of the multiplier is optimal under a frequency-independent scale prior and improves success probability by factors of 4.9 and 14.6 in the examples, while on logarithmic grids the architecture loses roughly the admissibility constant over the squared spectral peak times the log scale range relative to the bound. A Fourier-basis measurement of the input followed by classical randomization exactly reproduces the flag and scale outcomes of every such heralded circuit, making it at least as informative for global scale energies, as confirmed by a Hurst-exponent simulation. The QCWT's distinctive content is the joint scale–translation law: two chirps with identical Fourier- and time-basis measurement laws differ in QCWT law at total-variation distance 0.27.
AI.conclusion: Heralded QCWT circuits are well characterized by a tight success-probability bound reached by frequency-conditioned scale preparation, with per-scale multiplier normalization optimal for frequency-independent priors. However, for global scale energies all such circuits are no more informative than a Fourier-basis measurement plus classical randomization; the QCWT's genuine advantage lies in the joint scale–translation distribution, which can distinguish signals indistinguishable in both Fourier and time bases.

title: Characterizing a neutral atom quantum simulator accessible in cloud
summary: Quantum simulators have become a reality in recent years, with several platforms now remotely accessible through the cloud. These systems give researchers the opportunity to run quantum programs without requiring either a dedicated laboratory or extensive experimental expertise, and, in several cases, they have already enabled the execution of relevant protocols with remarkable results. However, despite the impressive progress in the performance of these machines, they still suffer from various noise sources, some of which are not always completely clear to the end user, which limits their applicability to tasks that are sufficiently robust against noise of various kinds. In this work, we investigate the behavior of Fresnel, a remotely accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator provided by Pasqal. We design and perform a series of experiments probing the machine's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings, and identify the main noise sources affecting its dynamics. Based on these data, we construct an effective model of the system's noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths. The resulting model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, showing how effective noise models can be built for cloud-based quantum resources.

AI.tldr: The authors characterize the noise of Pasqal's cloud-accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator "Fresnel" by running designed pulse-sequence experiments, identifying dominant noise sources, and inferring noise strengths via numerical optimization to build an effective noise model that reproduces the simulator's dynamics.
AI.motivation: Cloud-based quantum simulators are increasingly used but suffer from noise sources that are not fully transparent to end users, restricting their applicability to noise-robust tasks; users need reliable effective noise models for such remote resources.
AI.method: They design and execute a series of experiments probing Fresnel's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings to identify the main noise sources, then construct an effective model of the noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths.
AI.result: The inferred effective noise model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, and the main noise sources affecting the device are identified.
AI.conclusion: Effective noise models can be systematically built for cloud-based quantum resources through targeted experiments plus optimization-based parameter inference, improving transparency and usability of remote quantum simulators.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Maps on a Quantum Computer: Spectral Filtering and Galerkin PDE Solvers
summary: Diffusion maps generalize principal component analysis (PCA) to nonlinear manifolds, enabling spectral dimensionality reduction, geometric data analysis, and elliptic PDE approximation on point clouds. For large datasets of size $N$, however, classical matrix operations incur prohibitive $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ scaling, even when extracting low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables. We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework that bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by exploiting the symmetric factorization $G = A^T A$ directly at the block-encoding level. Combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), we implement spectral filters of $A$ to estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, as well as to prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction further allows the block-encoding queries to be used across multiple scalar observables. Under polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to $A$ and state-preparation oracles, our heat-overlap algorithm achieves $O(\operatorname{polylog} N)$ gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate our discrete circuit constructions, while a matched approximate-counting benchmark demonstrates the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithmic framework computes diffusion-map spectral quantities (heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, energy responses, and Galerkin solution states) directly from the symmetric factorization G = A^T A at the block-encoding level, avoiding explicit graph-Laplacian assembly and achieving polylog(N) complexity.
AI.motivation: Classical diffusion maps generalize PCA to nonlinear manifolds but require poly(N) matrix operations for large datasets, even when only low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables are needed. The authors seek N-independent (polylogarithmic) scaling by leveraging quantum linear-algebra primitives.
AI.method: The framework bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian construction by exploiting the symmetric factorization G = A^T A at the block-encoding level. It combines Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) to implement spectral filters of A. These filters estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, and prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction lets one block-encoding query serve multiple scalar observables.
AI.result: Given polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to A and state-preparation oracles, the heat-overlap algorithm attains O(polylog N) gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate the discrete circuit constructions, and a matched approximate-counting benchmark shows the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.
AI.conclusion: Quantum spectral filtering of the factorized diffusion operator enables polylog(N) diffusion-map computations on point clouds, with ideal-simulation and benchmarking evidence supporting correctness and a coherent-sampling precision advantage.

title: Analytic and Numerical Investigation of a Proposed Non-linear Extension of Quantum Mechanics
summary: In this paper, additional properties of a previously introduced non-linear extension of quantum mechanics are investigated. Analytically, we uncover a limit in which the model reduces to ordinary linear quantum mechanics. We also perform a perturbation analysis about an exact solution studied in earlier work. The equations represent a system that is subject to a periodic driver, and we use Floquet theory to help determine its properties. Numerically, we compare the exact solution to the analytic approximation, and we exhibit several examples of how the non-linear effects influence particle trajectories, with particular emphasis on trajectories near the linear limit.

AI.tldr: This paper studies additional properties of a previously proposed non-linear extension of quantum mechanics, showing analytically that the model admits a limit reducing to ordinary linear quantum mechanics, and perturbatively analyzing an exact solution under a periodic driver using Floquet theory, with numerical comparison of exact versus approximate results.
AI.motivation: The work aims to characterize a previously introduced non-linear quantum-mechanical model more fully—specifically its relationship to standard linear quantum mechanics and the behavior of its solutions under a periodic driving term.
AI.method: An analytic identification of a limit in which the model reduces to linear quantum mechanics; a perturbation analysis about a previously studied exact solution; Floquet theory applied to the periodically driven system to determine its properties; and numerical comparison of the exact solution with the analytic approximation, focused on particle trajectories near the linear limit.
AI.result: A linear-limit reduction of the non-linear model is uncovered analytically, the perturbation expansion around the exact driven solution is obtained with Floquet-theoretic characterization, and several examples illustrate how the non-linear effects modify particle trajectories, especially near the linear limit.
AI.conclusion: The non-linear extension contains ordinary linear quantum mechanics as a limiting case, and its perturbative and Floquet analysis, validated numerically, provides a quantitative picture of how non-linearity deforms trajectories—most transparently in the near-linear regime.

title: Tunable source of entangled microwaves by nonlinear scattering of magnons
summary: We propose a route to prepare entangled states of microwaves propagating in spatially separated transmission lines using the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of ferromagnetic spin waves (magnons). We first show that a driven magnon mode can produce entangled magnon pairs at low temperatures by spontaneous parametric down-conversion enabled by three-magnon processes. The anisotropic magnon properties in thin films result in strict phase-matching conditions which allow only a well-defined pair of magnon modes to be amplified. This mode selectivity allows to out-couple each amplified mode to an independent microwave transmission line, producing non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement with current experimental parameters. In addition, we prove that the frequency difference between the two entangled microwaves can be dynamically tuned across a few-GHz range by changing the orientation of a bias magnetic field. Our figures of merit - .g., the amount of microwave entanglement - can be largely improved by optimizing material and geometry. Our work establishes that quantum states of propagating magnons can be created by their nonlinear dynamics alone, and opens a pathway toward integrating magnons in hybrid quantum platforms.

AI.tldr: The authors propose generating entangled propagating microwave states in spatially separated transmission lines by exploiting the intrinsic three-magnon nonlinear dynamics of ferromagnetic spin waves, with tunable non-degenerate frequency splitting.
AI.motivation: Entangled propagating microwaves are valuable resources for quantum information, but generating non-degenerate entanglement across separated channels using a compact, integrable platform remains challenging. Magnons offer strong nonlinearities and compatibility with hybrid quantum systems, motivating a magnon-based entanglement source.
AI.method: A driven magnon mode undergoes spontaneous parametric down-conversion via three-magnon processes at low temperature, producing entangled magnon pairs. Anisotropy of magnons in thin films imposes strict phase-matching, selecting a well-defined pair of amplified modes. Each amplified mode is out-coupled to an independent microwave transmission line, yielding non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement. The frequency difference is tuned over a few-GHz range by reorienting the bias magnetic field.
AI.result: Non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement is achievable with current experimental parameters. The frequency splitting of the entangled microwaves is dynamically tunable across a few-GHz range via bias-field orientation, and figures of merit (e.g., amount of entanglement) can be substantially improved through material and geometry optimization.
AI.conclusion: Quantum states of propagating magnons can be created by their nonlinear dynamics alone, establishing magnons as an integrable resource for entanglement generation and opening a pathway toward magnon-based hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Certified Separation Between Coherent and Adaptive Temporal Processing of Quantum-Error-Correction Readout
summary: Repeated quantum-error-correction readout is normally converted into a classical time series: each syndrome pulse is measured on arrival and only the resulting classical record is retained. Nonorthogonal readout signals raise the question of whether preserving quantum information between rounds can improve the final recovery decision. We formulate this comparison as a loss-weighted state-discrimination problem. For an idealized two-round benchmark with quadrature phase-shift-keying (QPSK) signals, a receiver with a seven-dimensional persistent register has certified recovery-decision error below $24.2100\%$, whereas every separate adaptive receiver has error above $25.1431\%$. The certified separation is at least $0.933$ percentage points. The loss counts incorrect final error-mask decisions in the benchmark. In the strict architecture, where the counted register is the entire persistent state, four dimensions are necessary and sufficient to outperform the adaptive class. Certified separations also occur at three and four rounds with register dimensions $8$ and $36$, compared with $16$ and $64$ for full-prefix storage. We relate memory dimension to the structure of the temporal measurement, give a sufficient memory bound for collective measurements, and quantify robustness to register dephasing and accumulated channel error.

AI.tldr: A receiver that keeps a small persistent quantum register (e.g., 7 dimensions for two-round QPSK) can make final error-mask decisions with certified lower error than any separate adaptive classical-readout receiver; four dimensions are necessary and sufficient in the strict architecture.
AI.motivation: Repeated QEC readout discards quantum information by converting syndromes into a classical time series. Since readout signals are nonorthogonal, retaining quantum information across rounds may improve the final recovery decision, so the paper asks whether and how much a quantum-persistent memory helps.
AI.method: Formulates the comparison as a loss-weighted state-discrimination problem. Uses an idealized two-round QPSK benchmark, certifies error bounds for a seven-dimensional persistent-register receiver versus separate adaptive receivers, and analyzes the strict architecture (counted register = entire persistent state) to find necessary and sufficient dimensions. Extends to three and four rounds and derives a sufficient memory bound for collective measurements, plus robustness to dephasing and accumulated channel error.
AI.result: Two-round QPSK: persistent receiver error below 24.2100% vs. above 25.1431% for every separate adaptive receiver, a certified separation of at least 0.933 percentage points. Four dimensions are necessary and sufficient to beat the adaptive class; full-prefix storage would need 16. For three and four rounds, certified separations occur with dimensions 8 and 36 vs. 16 and 64 for full-prefix storage.
AI.conclusion: Preserving a modest amount of quantum information between readout rounds yields certified improvement in recovery decisions, with memory dimension tied to the temporal measurement structure; the results hold under dephasing and accumulated channel error.

title: Resilience of emergent Hamiltonian quantum memories in the presence of noise
summary: Emergent Hamiltonians can freeze an entangled state prepared through coherent evolution, since that state is an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian under which it is then stored. We show that the freedom left in this construction allows the storage spectrum to be adapted to a noisy environment without changing the stored state. For a product of Bell pairs prepared from a density wave in an engineered chain, a selection rule prevents local density noise from connecting the target to any of its degenerate partners, so that rescaling the storage Hamiltonian by a factor $α$ moves every transition this noise drives. Under $1/f$ noise, the storage time then grows in proportion to $α$, a result we confirm by evolving the memory under explicit classical $1/f$ fields, whereas for an Ohmic bath the most favorable scale depends on its cutoff. Fermionic loss, treated as a solvable model, includes a transition that rescaling leaves at zero frequency, and an energy shift $μ$ per particle moves it away from zero, with an exact orbital solution giving the resulting lifetimes. Finally, among number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians, $α$ and $μ$ are the only controls that keep the storage Hamiltonian nearest neighbor at every time along the preparation, so that the protocol combines local freezing with control over the storage spectrum.

AI.tldr: Emergent (parent) Hamiltonians can freeze a coherently prepared entangled state since it becomes their eigenstate; the residual freedom in this construction is used to tune the storage spectrum—without altering the stored state—so it is optimally decoupled from a given noise environment.
AI.motivation: States prepared by coherent evolution are eigenstates of the emergent Hamiltonian under which they are stored, which "freezes" them, but a practical memory still decoheres due to noise-driven transitions to degenerate or nearby states. The goal is to exploit the leftover freedom in the emergent-Hamiltonian construction to protect the stored state against specific noise sources rather than accept a fixed, unprotected spectrum.
AI.method: The protocol is developed analytically for a density-wave-prepared chain whose target is a product of Bell pairs: a selection rule forbids local density noise from connecting the target to its degenerate partners, so rescaling the storage Hamiltonian by α rigidly shifts all noise-driven transitions. Dynamics are simulated under explicit classical 1/f fields and for an Ohmic bath; fermionic loss is treated as a solvable model with an exact orbital solution, and an energy shift μ per particle is added to move the residual zero-frequency transition. Constraints from number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians are analyzed to identify admissible controls.
AI.result: Under 1/f noise the storage time grows linearly with α (confirmed by explicit classical-field evolution), while for an Ohmic bath the optimal scale depends on the cutoff. In the fermionic-loss model, rescaling alone leaves one transition pinned at zero frequency; an energy shift μ per particle displaces it, and the exact orbital solution yields the resulting lifetimes. Among number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians, α and μ are the only controls that keep the storage Hamiltonian nearest-neighbor at all times during preparation.
AI.conclusion: Emergent-Hamiltonian freezing need not come at the cost of a rigid, noise-mismatched spectrum: state-preserving rescaling (α) and chemical-potential-like shift (μ) provide a minimal, experimentally compatible knob set that tunes the storage spectrum for enhanced lifetimes while preserving locality (nearest-neighbor structure) throughout preparation and storage.

title: Quantum dynamical transitions when the corresponding classical phase space has a separatrix: extension of the QKNH theorem beyond double wells
summary: In classical Hamiltonian systems with a slowly time-dependent parameter, adiabaticity breaks down at a separatrix, leading to probabilistic post-adiabatic transitions between different phase-space regions described by the Kruskal-Neishtadt-Henrard (KNH) theorem. Quantum mechanically, dynamical tunneling allows adiabaticity to persist where it breaks down classically, making the quantum-classical correspondence for separatrix crossing non-trivial. We recently established a quantum version of the KNH theorem (QKNH) by introducing the concept of a sweep-rate-dependent quantum separatrix in the instantaneous energy spectrum of the time-dependent system. The QKNH theorem relates the splitting of a quantum ensemble between the outgoing dynamical sectors at the quantum separatrix to their relative growth rates, and thus provides a quantum analog of the classical KNH rule. Here, we demonstrate that these findings are not restricted to double-well systems with tunneling through a potential barrier. We investigate a slowly driven quantum pendulum, in which the avoided crossings arise from above-barrier reflection. The resulting Landau-Zener probabilities have the same local lattice form as in the double-well problem, allowing the application of the QKNH theorem.

AI.tldr: The authors show that the previously established quantum Kruskal-Neishtadt-Henrard (QKNH) theorem, developed for double-well systems, extends to a slowly driven quantum pendulum where avoided crossings originate from above-barrier reflection; the resulting Landau-Zener probabilities exhibit the same local lattice structure, enabling application of the QKNH rule.
AI.motivation: In classical systems with a slowly time-dependent parameter, adiabaticity breaks down at a separatrix and post-adiabatic branching follows the KNH theorem. Quantum mechanically, dynamical tunneling can sustain adiabaticity where the classical description fails, making the quantum-classical correspondence at separatrix crossing non-trivial. The recently proposed QKNH theorem addressed this for double-well systems, but it was unclear whether the framework is generic or specific to tunneling through a potential barrier.
AI.method: The paper investigates a slowly driven quantum pendulum, a system in which the relevant avoided crossings arise from above-barrier reflection rather than barrier tunneling. The authors analyze the instantaneous energy spectrum, introduce a sweep-rate-dependent quantum separatrix, and compute the associated Landau-Zener transition probabilities, examining their structure for comparison with the double-well case.
AI.result: The Landau-Zener probabilities in the driven quantum pendulum display the same local lattice form as those found in the double-well problem.
