This shared structure permits the QKNH theorem to be applied, linking the splitting of a quantum ensemble among outgoing dynamical sectors at the quantum separatrix to their relative growth rates.
AI.conclusion: The QKNH theorem is not restricted to double-well systems with tunneling through a potential barrier but extends to systems whose avoided crossings stem from above-barrier reflection. This indicates that the quantum separatrix-crossing framework is generic, based on the lattice structure of Landau-Zener probabilities rather than on the specific physical origin of the avoided crossings.

title: Generation of coherent-state Schrödinger cat states in a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model implemented with Josephson junctions
summary: We investigate the generation of coherent-state Schrödinger cat states using a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) implemented in a Josephson-junction quantum circuit. We consider a specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation and estimate the resulting two-photon coupling constant. We numerically examine three types of noise: magnetic flux noise with $1/f$ fluctuations, energy relaxation associated with the flux-qubit $T_{1}$ decay, and photon loss in the bosonic mode obtained by quantizing the phase variable of the dc SQUID used for qubit readout. We find that photon loss has a particularly significant effect on cat-state fidelity. We also investigate the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for the $l$-photon JCM ($l=1,2,3,4$), starting from a coherent bosonic state. Finally, we assume that the bosonic mode is initially prepared in a displaced thermal state and then decoupled from the heat bath. We study the subsequent unitary evolution to determine how the initial temperature affects the fidelity and Wigner function of the generated cat states.

AI.tldr: The paper studies coherent-state Schrödinger cat state generation via a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model in a superconducting flux-qubit circuit, numerically evaluating magnetic flux noise, qubit relaxation, and photon loss, and analyzing phase-space and thermal effects on cat-state fidelity.
AI.motivation: Schrödinger cat states are valuable resources for quantum information, and implementing multi-photon Jaynes-Cummings interactions in superconducting circuits offers a route to generate them; however, realistic noise sources and initial thermal occupation threaten fidelity, motivating a quantitative noise and initialization study.
AI.method: The authors consider a specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation of the two-photon JCM and estimate the two-photon coupling constant. They numerically simulate three noise channels: 1/f magnetic flux noise, flux-qubit T1 energy relaxation, and photon loss in the bosonic mode (obtained by quantizing the dc SQUID phase variable used for readout). They also track the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for l-photon JCM (l = 1-4) from an initial coherent state, and study unitary evolution from an initially displaced thermal state decoupled from the bath.
AI.result: Photon loss is found to affect cat-state fidelity particularly strongly compared with flux noise and qubit relaxation. The Pegg-Barnett phase-basis analysis characterizes the dynamics for l = 1-4. Starting from a displaced thermal state, the initial temperature measurably degrades the fidelity and distorts the Wigner function of the generated cat states.
AI.conclusion: Photon loss is the dominant decoherence channel for cat-state generation in this two-photon JCM flux-qubit architecture, and residual initial thermal occupation further limits fidelity and Wigner-function quality, indicating that cavity loss control and ground-state cooling are priorities for practical implementation.

title: Curvature-Calibrated Friction and an Exact Gauge Symmetry for Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027), IEEE Symposium for Multidisciplinary Computational Intelligence Incubators (IEEE MCII). Code: https://github.com/khoshisashi/qhd-curvature-friction
summary: A design problem constrained by a partial differential equation can be solved coherently on a quantum computer. The objective is block-encoded rather than measured, and Quantum Hamiltonian Descent consumes it directly. We identify two obstacles in this pipeline and repair both. First, the oracle construction assumes affine generators with positive semidefinite Hermitian parts, which covariance entries violate for every off-diagonal generator. Encoding the covariance as an affine combination of positive semidefinite atoms restores both conditions at every register point, at the price of a representational floor, median 45% of the fitted family's own objective range for a fixed rank-three dictionary and 22% with a variable diagonal. Second, adding a constant to the objective leaves the measurement distribution exactly invariant, yet the mean-objective friction heuristic in current use assigns such objectives different schedules. Calibrating the friction to the landscape curvature restores the symmetry, though not the constant in $ν= c\sqrtμ$, and a bracketed sweep at matched objective-phase exposure, not end-to-end cost, places the best tested friction between 0.032 and 0.25 of critical damping on a diffusion-design benchmark, a broad plateau an order of magnitude below the classical default.

AI.tldr: Two defects in the PDE-constrained design pipeline for Quantum Hamiltonian Descent are identified and repaired: non-affine covariance generators are re-expressed as affine combinations of PSD atoms, and the mean-objective friction heuristic is replaced by curvature calibration; the best friction sits far below classical default.
AI.motivation: Design problems constrained by PDEs can in principle be solved coherently on a quantum computer by block-encoding the objective and feeding it directly to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD), avoiding measurement. The authors show this pipeline is broken in two places: the oracle construction requires affine generators with positive semidefinite Hermitian parts, which covariance entries violate for every off-diagonal generator; and the friction heuristic is not invariant to adding a constant to the objective, even though the measurement distribution is.
AI.method: Obstacle 1 is fixed by encoding the covariance as an affine combination of positive semidefinite atoms, restoring both required conditions at every register point. Obstacle 2 is fixed by calibrating the friction coefficient to the landscape curvature rather than to the mean objective. The friction sweep is bracketed at matched objective-phase exposure rather than end-to-end cost, and tested on a diffusion-design benchmark.
AI.result: The atom decomposition incurs a representational floor: median 45% of the fitted family's own objective range for a fixed rank-three dictionary, and 22% with a variable diagonal. Curvature calibration restores the constant-shift symmetry of the schedule but does not recover the constant in the relation ν = c√μ. On the diffusion-design benchmark, the best tested friction lies between 0.032 and 0.25 of critical damping, forming a broad plateau roughly an order of magnitude below the classical default.
AI.conclusion: Both pipeline obstacles are repairable, but each repair carries a cost: a nontrivial representational floor from the PSD atom decomposition, and an incomplete symmetry restoration in the friction calibration. The practical finding is that near-critical-damping friction well below the classical default suffices across a wide plateau, so tuning need not be sharp.

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
summary: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.

AI.tldr: A basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization maps the RVE reduced finite-element energy to a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian; using the Hellmann–Feynman theorem the homogenized stress reduces to one-local Pauli-Z observables measurable in the same computational basis as the energy.
AI.motivation: Computational homogenization demands repeated RVE solves to obtain effective macroscale response including homogenized stress, which is computationally expensive. A quantum formulation could offer a variational route to the equilibrium fluctuation field and its stress observables.
AI.method: Express the reduced finite-element energy of the RVE as a QUBO and map it to an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state is the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Differentiate the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to prescribed macroscopic strain via the Hellmann–Feynman theorem to obtain stress observables. Approximate ground states with VQE; demonstrate on a 2D periodic RVE.
AI.result: Although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local: in linear elasticity the two-qubit couplings are strain-independent, so differentiation eliminates all two-qubit terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-Z operators. These are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian, so homogenized stress is extracted directly from the optimized state using the same computational-basis measurements, without reconstructing the microscopic displacement field or adding a measurement basis. Demonstrated on a 2D periodic RVE.
AI.conclusion: The formulation yields homogenized stress directly from VQE-optimized states via shared computational-basis measurements, avoiding displacement-field reconstruction and extra measurement bases, establishing a structurally efficient quantum workflow for linear-elastic computational homogenization.

title: Counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise: dependence on trajectory pairing
summary: Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.

AI.tldr: Attribution of quantum error-correction failures to underlying noise is pairing-dependent under non-Pauli noise. The authors define "cause sets" (sites whose removal alone removes a failure), separate them from pairing-independent net effects, and show that in a distance-three surface code exact coherent noise and its Pauli twirl are nearly indistinguishable by pairing-independent metrics yet sharply differ in cause-set structure under shared random draws.
AI.motivation: Under Pauli noise, attributing a stabilizer-code failure to its causal noise has a canonical answer, but under non-Pauli (coherent) noise the answer depends on how noise trajectories are paired with counterfactuals. The paper aims to formalize this ambiguity and provide an attribution framework that is well-defined and honestly reported.
AI.method: They define a failing shot's cause set as the set of sites whose removal alone eliminates the failure, and distinguish these from pairing-independent net effects. Pairing is shown to enter wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making pairing maximal at every random step yields shared random numbers, whereas continuity-based pairings do not. They compare exact non-Pauli noise against its Pauli twirl in a distance-three surface code across admissible pairings, examining cause-set sizes and mean coherent cause counts.
AI.result: Exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures require three or more sites versus 2.3% under the twirl. Different admissible pairings shift the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 up to 80 times the marginal-allowed minimum, while pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models.
AI.conclusion: Cause-set attribution under non-Pauli noise is fundamentally pairing-dependent, so no single canonical attribution exists. Shot-level attributions should explicitly state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside, since these alone do not distinguish exact coherent noise from its Pauli twirl.

title: Interfacing Silicon Nitride Nanophotonics with Cuprous Oxide Rydberg Excitons
summary: Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O), the solid-state counterpart of Rydberg atoms, are hydrogen-like electron--hole quasi-particles with micron-sized wavefunctions and strong long-range interactions that promise optical nonlinearities at the few-photon level. Exploiting them in a waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) setting can enable what atomic Rydberg platforms achieve only with ultrahigh vacuum and laser cooling/trapping---a guided optical mode interfaced with the Rydberg medium---while adding the scalability and advanced fabrication of integrated photonics. Here we demonstrate a monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface of Cu$_2$O Rydberg excitons with a SiN$_x$ nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission from the Cu$_2$O microcrystal is coupled to the guided mode, routed along the waveguide, and collected from an output grating. The spectrum shows the phonon-assisted 1$s$ orthoexciton emission together with the low-lying 2$p$ and 3$p$ lines of the yellow Rydberg series. Spatially selective excitation excludes substrate background and direct scatter, and the enhanced linear polarization of the grating-collected signal identifies the TE-like guided mode as the collection channel. These results establish the complete material--device--measurement stack for a novel platform of nonlinear quantum nanophotonics based on Rydberg excitons.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of a monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface coupling Cu2O Rydberg excitons to a SiNx nanophotonic waveguide, with excitonic emission routed along the waveguide and collected from an output grating, establishes the material-device-measurement stack for Rydberg-exciton nonlinear quantum nanophotonics.
AI.motivation: Rydberg excitons in Cu2O are solid-state analogs of Rydberg atoms with micron-sized wavefunctions and strong long-range interactions, promising few-photon optical nonlinearities. Embedding them in a waveguide QED setting could deliver what atomic Rydberg platforms require ultrahigh vacuum and laser cooling for, while adding integrated-photonics scalability.
AI.method: A Cu2O microcrystal is monolithically interfaced with a SiNx nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission is coupled into the guided mode, routed to an output grating, and collected. Spatially selective excitation suppresses substrate background and direct scatter; polarization analysis identifies the TE-like guided mode as the collection channel.
AI.result: The collected spectrum shows phonon-assisted 1s orthoexciton emission along with the low-lying 2p and 3p lines of the yellow Rydberg series; enhanced linear polarization of the grating-collected signal confirms TE-like guided-mode collection.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a complete material-device-measurement stack for a new platform of nonlinear quantum nanophotonics based on Rydberg excitons.

title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
summary: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.

AI.tldr: The paper converts measurements that detect correlation between a hidden system and a reference into binary hypothesis tests, yielding one-shot bounds on the convex-split lemma, trace distance, and hypothesis-testing relative entropy, and applies them to private communication and secret-key distillation.
AI.motivation: To quantify how many independent quantum systems are needed to hide a system correlated with a reference, so as to control decorrelation and decoupling arguments that underpin one-shot private communication and one-way secret-key distillation.
AI.method: Any joint measurement on the reference and the hidden system is turned into binary tests on a single system plus the reference. For each test the probability of declaring a signal under an independent (product) preparation is bounded; averaging the largest admissible signal-acceptance probabilities controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound derives the sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the reference state. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces, and comparing two distributions for the hidden system's location yields one-shot bounds incorporating eavesdropper public information.
AI.result: The bounds give one-shot results for private communication and one-way secret-key distillation. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, the Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from n repetitions are recovered, with remaining loss bounded by log2 n + O(1) at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound using O(n) public bits.
AI.conclusion: Hypothesis-testing techniques on a single system plus reference yield tight, one-shot characterizations of hiding correlated systems via the convex-split lemma, and these translate into near-optimal private communication and secret-key rates with only logarithmic loss at the second order, achievable by position-based protocols with linear public communication.

title: Remote Use of Quantum Machines in the Adversarial Scenario
summary: Networked quantum technologies allow users to operate quantum machines hosted by remote servers, but classical commands alone cannot ensure that only the intended user can prepare the useful inputs that activate them. We formulate the problem of adversarial remote use of quantum machines in the framework of quantum resource theories. A device controlled by Bob is correlated to a remote user, Alice, through a bipartite state, and also to an adversary Eve holding its purification. Alice and Eve compete to programme Bob's machine by remotely preparing its inputs: the conditional state carries the quantum resource, while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. Remote use is truly advantageous when Alice is guaranteed to unlock a larger average task value than the adversary Eve, given the same marginal state of Bob. We show that for tasks with a convex figure of merit, the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs and, for spectral tasks, where the figure of merit is invariant under unitary operations, by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation show that the same noisy state may secure exclusivity one machine but not another. Finally, we order Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers through a task-independent simulation preorder, based on the ensembles each party can prepare on Bob's side. Shared quantum correlations thereby become a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes adversarial remote use of quantum machines via quantum resource theories, showing that exclusivity of access is governed by complementary upper roofs (convex tasks) or an entanglement imbalance (spectral tasks), and orders Alice's and Eve's programming powers via a task-independent simulation preorder.
AI.motivation: Networked quantum technologies let users operate remotely hosted quantum machines, but classical authentication cannot guarantee that only the intended user can prepare the inputs that activate the device; a framework is needed to characterize when a legitimate remote user genuinely has exclusive programming access against an adversary.
AI.method: The problem is cast in quantum resource theories: a Bob-controlled device is correlated to remote user Alice through a bipartite state and to adversary Eve via its purification. Alice and Eve compete to programme Bob's inputs—the conditional state carries the quantum resource while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. Advantage is defined as Alice unlocking a larger average task value than Eve at the same marginal state of Bob; the analysis uses complementary upper roofs for convex figures of merit and an entanglement imbalance for spectral (unitarily invariant) tasks, plus a task-independent simulation preorder over the ensembles each party can prepare.
AI.result: For tasks with a convex figure of merit the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs; for spectral tasks it is governed by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Case studies—purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation—show that the same noisy state can secure exclusivity for one machine but not another.
AI.conclusion: Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers are ordered through a task-independent simulation preorder based on the ensembles each can prepare on Bob's side, establishing shared quantum correlations as a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.

title: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
summary:
We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states.
  We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is $\mathsf{RE}$-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.

AI.tldr: The paper maps the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from fixed points of bounded-degree bosonic Lindbladians, showing a landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and RE-hardness of stationarity itself.
AI.motivation: While transient bosonic dynamics complexity is understood, the computational power of bosonic stationary states is open, requiring treatment of infinite-dimensional subtleties: existence, uniqueness, and convergence of fixed points.
AI.method: Complexity-theoretic reductions and constructions for bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions, including embedding quantum circuits into fixed-point observable estimation, classical simulatability arguments for Gaussian regimes, and hardness reductions from boson-sampling conjectures and RE-hardness proofs via degree-five jump operators on four modes.
AI.result: Universal quantum computation embeds into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a degree-twelve-Hamiltonian Lindbladian with only linear photon loss, preparable from vacuum in polynomial time; Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping are efficiently classically samplable and stable under weak Kerr perturbations; Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping are hard to sample exactly under constant-rate loss and hard to approximate at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures; non-Gaussian fixed-point sampling relates to boson-sampling variants; deciding existence of a stationary density operator is RE-hard even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators on at most four modes.
AI.conclusion: Bosonic fixed points exhibit a rich complexity phase structure, from universal quantum computational power to classical simulability and undecidability, with dissipative bosonic steady states serving as a versatile resource and a source of hardness.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing
summary: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.

AI.tldr: A unified algorithmic framework for sensing time-dependent AC fields, combining new pulse-sequence protocols (randomized, matched, pooled spectroscopy) that hit optimal sensitivity on conventional sensors, and quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS) that couples a quantum sensor to a quantum processor to reach a polynomial-beyond-Heisenberg limit robust to aligned depolarizing noise.
AI.motivation: Conventional AC sensing (e.g., dynamical decoupling) is limited in sensitivity, and existing theory offers no algorithmic account of how to design optimal sensing protocols. The authors aim to establish an algorithmic theory of sensing and to determine whether quantum computation can fundamentally surpass conventional sensing limits, especially under realistic noise.
AI.method: Three pulse-sequence protocols are developed: randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, evaluated against established schemes such as dynamical decoupling. The authors then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples a quantum sensor to a quantum processor via two primitives: (i) a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and (ii) a family of quantum algorithms that extract signal information from the oracle in superposition. Implementations require only one memory ancilla.
AI.result: The three pulse protocols outperform established approaches across a wide range of tasks and attain optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin/qubit platforms by changing only pulse sequences. QCS achieves a limit polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, establishing a separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Under constant-strength sensor depolarization aligned with the signal, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals, whereas any protocol lacking quantum computation is proven to be limited to standard-quantum-limit scaling.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first asymptotic beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology under signal-aligned noise, showing Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. It builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and positions quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with advantages surpassing the Heisenberg limit and persisting under noise.

title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
summary: We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.

AI.tldr: GEARS is a runtime calibration framework that amplifies gate errors to obtain stronger syndrome-based signals for in situ recalibration of quantum error correction, cutting measurement needs ~8x and excess logical failures by 31–40%.
AI.motivation: Long computations on large qubit arrays require repeated calibration against hardware drift. Conventional calibration removes qubits from the code (space-time overhead), while syndrome-based in situ recalibration is limited by a trade-off: more measurements slow control updates, and stronger probes increase calibration signal but inject extra errors.
AI.method: GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with gate-error amplification: it repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while bounding the logical cost of probing. Evaluated via surface code simulations with depth-three amplification.
AI.result: Depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by ~8x at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, excess expected logical failures drop by ~31–40% over evaluated execution windows; under time-dependent drift, the estimated critical drift frequency increases ~1.9x.
AI.conclusion: Deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation is a viable strategy for improving long-time performance of quantum computations through more efficient in situ recalibration.

title: Insurance portfolio simulation with a quantum circuit
summary: A central challenge in actuarial science is characterising the distribution of losses generated by an insurance portfolio. Copulas provide a natural framework for modelling joint distributions, but flexible high-dimensional copula fitting and sampling remains challenging in practice. We propose a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) approach adapted to insurance portfolios, combining (i) a tail-focused discretisation of heavy-tailed marginals, (ii) a Monte Carlo-style objective function that enables the numerical precision of the algorithm to scale when trained on a relatively small number of samples, and (iii) a two-stage hierarchical training scheme enabling efficient training on a simulator and fine-tuning on quantum hardware. On a mixed portfolio of equity returns and insurance losses, the trained circuit recovers the qualitative dependence structure, with near-independence between equity and losses and positive dependence among loss lines. Exponential quantile encoding substantially improves the fit to the tail of the aggregate loss distribution relative to a uniform encoding, and the hierarchical scheme substantially outperforms single-stage training of a circuit of the same size from random initialisation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) for fitting and sampling high-dimensional copulas of insurance portfolios, using tail-focused heavy-tail discretisation, a Monte Carlo-style objective, and hierarchical training.
AI.motivation: Characterising loss distributions of insurance portfolios is a central actuarial challenge; copulas suit joint-distribution modelling but flexible high-dimensional fitting and sampling remain practically difficult.
AI.method: A QCBM adapted to insurance portfolios combining (i) tail-focused discretisation of heavy-tailed marginals (exponential quantile encoding), (ii) a Monte Carlo-style objective letting numerical precision scale with relatively few training samples, and (iii) a two-stage hierarchical training scheme: simulator pre-training followed by hardware fine-tuning.
AI.result: On a mixed portfolio of equity returns and insurance losses, the trained circuit recovers the qualitative dependence structure—near-independence between equity and losses, positive dependence among loss lines. Exponential quantile encoding markedly improves tail fit of the aggregate loss distribution over uniform encoding, and hierarchical training substantially outperforms single-stage training of an equal-size circuit from random initialisation.
AI.conclusion: The QCBM with tail-focused encoding and hierarchical training is a viable, hardware-compatible approach for high-dimensional copula modelling of insurance portfolios, particularly for aggregate-loss tails.

title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a simultaneous (transversal) controlled-Z gate across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture, using a tailored dynamical decoupling scheme with a genuine geometric cancellation that lowers pulse count and, for selected register sizes, outperforms sequential two-qubit gates in speed while requiring much lower two-photon Rabi frequency. Experimental feasibility is assessed via decoherence and crosstalk from laser wave-vector misalignment, and crosstalk-induced errors are studied in fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state across two [[4,1,2]] code blocks.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing demands high-fidelity entangling gates that can be applied efficiently across many qubit pairs at once. Sequential two-qubit gates are slow and resource-intensive, motivating parallel (transversal) entangling operations in scalable trapped-ion architectures.
AI.method: A scheme for simultaneous pairwise controlled-Z operations across neighboring wells of a double-well trapped-ion register. A tailored dynamical decoupling sequence suppresses unwanted couplings, originally scaling quadratically with ion number; a genuine geometric cancellation is introduced to reduce pulse count. Feasibility is evaluated by modeling decoherence and crosstalk from laser wave-vector misalignment, and by simulating crosstalk-induced gate errors in fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two [[4,1,2]] quantum-error-detection code blocks.
AI.result: The geometric cancellation reduces the required pulse count and, for selected register sizes, completes the parallel operation faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while needing a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. Decoherence and crosstalk analyses quantify realistic imperfections, and simulations show how crosstalk-induced gate errors degrade fault-tolerant logical Bell-state preparation across two [[4,1,2]] code blocks.
AI.conclusion: Transversal entangling gates are a viable building block for scalable, trapped-ion-based fault-tolerant quantum error correction, with the proposed scheme offering pulse-count, speed, and Rabi-frequency advantages validated against realistic decoherence and crosstalk imperfections.

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that, for supervised binary classification with noisy parameterized quantum circuits, boosting avoids the superpolynomial PEC sampling overhead by exploiting label/margin information, requiring fewer circuit executions as depth and noise grow while matching test accuracy.
AI.motivation: Quantum error mitigation (QEM), particularly probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), can require superpolynomial sampling overhead for general circuits, and no problem-agnostic approach escapes this. However, classification depends only on the sign and margin of the classifier output, not on exact reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value, suggesting problem-specific (label) information may reduce sampling cost.
AI.method: The authors build a theoretical and empirical framework comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits against PEC under the same learning target. For specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, they derive a shared hypothesis-class complexity bound linking empirical margin loss to expected classification risk, and establish resource criteria. Finite-shot teacher-student simulations evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost across circuit depth and physical noise strength.
AI.result: Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions than PEC, with the advantage growing as depth and noise increase, and it attains higher test accuracy than the reference method.
AI.conclusion: For the supervised-learning problems studied, there is a task-dependent resource advantage: leveraging information retained in noisy outputs avoids the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

title: Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Differential Privacy
summary:
Differential privacy has been successfully extended to quantum computing and information processing, where sensitive data are encoded in quantum states and protected by quantum noise mechanisms that keep the outcomes of any measurement on neighboring states nearly indistinguishable. In the quantum setting, however, the state submitted to a quantum computer may be entangled with a hidden reference system secretly held by an adversary. Such entanglement cannot be detected from the submitted state alone, and it poses a challenge with no counterpart in the classical setting. Existing frameworks of quantum differential privacy consider only measurements on the released state, leaving this scenario largely unexplored.
  In this paper, we identify the entanglement attack: an adversary submits one half of an entangled state to a quantum computer that runs a privacy mechanism, keeps the other half, and finally measures both halves jointly. We show that this attack may completely break a mechanism that satisfies quantum differential privacy with a finite parameter, driving its privacy parameter to infinity. To counter it, we propose entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP), a privacy framework that is native to quantum entanglement and remains valid against such attacks. We characterize exactly when a mechanism has a finite EA-QDP parameter, and show that the optimal parameter $\varepsilon^*_{\mathrm{EA}}$ of any quantum mechanism can be computed by a semidefinite programming problem (SDP). Building on this, we quantify the extra privacy leakage caused by entanglement and show that it can be bounded by choosing appropriate mechanisms, with the depolarizing channel being our recommended choice. Finally, we demonstrate both the attack and its countermeasure on simulated and physical quantum hardware, and the experimental results agree with our theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an entanglement attack that breaks standard quantum differential privacy (QDP) by entangling the submitted state with an adversary-held reference, and proposes entanglement-assisted QDP (EA-QDP) to remain robust against it.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum differential privacy frameworks only consider measurements on the released state, ignoring that the submitted quantum state may be entangled with a hidden reference system held by an adversary. This entanglement is undetectable from the submitted state alone and has no classical counterpart, leaving a serious gap in QDP guarantees.
AI.method: The authors formalize the entanglement attack, where an adversary submits one half of an entangled state to the quantum computer, retains the other half, and jointly measures both. They introduce entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP), characterize exactly when a mechanism has a finite EA-QDP parameter, and show that the optimal parameter epsilon*_EA can be computed via a semidefinite programming (SDP) problem. They also bound entanglement-induced privacy leakage and recommend the depolarizing channel.
AI.result: The entanglement attack can drive the privacy parameter of a QDP-satisfying mechanism to infinity, fully breaking it. EA-QDP remains valid against such attacks, its optimal parameter is computable by SDP, and extra privacy leakage from entanglement can be bounded by suitable mechanism choice (depolarizing channel). Results are validated on simulated and physical quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: Classical-style QDP is insufficient under adversarial entanglement, and EA-QDP provides a native, robust framework with computable guarantees and practical countermeasures, confirmed experimentally.

title: Structure-Guided Synthesis of Low-Error Syndrome Extraction Circuits
summary: Gate orders can change fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits implement the same ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing these orderings independently for every check, however, becomes computationally demanding as code size increases. We present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group, reducing independent ordering choices. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide the selection of the final circuit. We compare with state-of-the-art approaches, including Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome. Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, our method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates. Relative to ASC, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest is 38.6%. Our circuits improve circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserve the code distance in seven. Across five timed codes, our method reduces the mean time to the first feasible circuit by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC, at equal or lower depth.

AI.tldr: A CP-SAT-based synthesis method that shares relative gate orders across groups of recurring checks in structured CSS codes, jointly optimizing orders and gate timing to reduce logical error rates and drastically cut synthesis time versus ASC, PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome.
AI.motivation: Gate orderings affect fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits realize identical ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing orderings independently per check is computationally prohibitive as code size grows, so a scalable way to reduce the independent ordering choices is needed.
AI.method: The authors present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares a single relative gate order per group. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared gate orders and each physical gate's execution time, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the whole circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide selection of the final circuit.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15 quantum LDPC codes from ten code families, the method attains the lowest logical error rate estimates, with a median 11.4% and maximum 38.6% reduction relative to ASC (the strongest baseline). It improves circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserves the code distance in seven. On five timed codes, mean time to first feasible circuit is reduced by factors of 21.4-136.6 versus ASC at equal or lower depth.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting recurring check connectivity to share gate orders lets a CP-SAT formulation optimize syndrome-extraction circuits efficiently, simultaneously improving logical error rates and circuit-level distance while cutting synthesis runtime by over an order of magnitude compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: Nonmagnetic Impurity Effects on Majorana Braiding Quantum Gates in Vortex Cores
summary: Using time-dependent many-body simulations, we investigate nonmagnetic impurity effects on vortex-core Majorana braiding. In the two-MZM $\sqrt{Z}$ gate, sufficiently strong attractive impurities suppress the topological gap $Δ_t$, reduce adiabaticity, and degrade the quantization of the geometric-phase difference; the repulsive impurities considered here cause no comparable damage despite stronger zero-energy nonequilibrium local density of states (LDOS) distortions. Slowing the braid or using a $2a_0$ detour restores near-quantization in the cases examined. In the four-MZM configuration, attractive impurities leave the low-energy spectrum nearly unchanged, whereas repulsive impurities mainly suppress the first excited state. Slower braiding substantially improves the $X$ gate success probability. A specific attractive-impurity pair yields near-unit success ($\approx 0.9985$), unlike two weak repulsive impurities. These findings clarify how nonmagnetic impurities affect the low-energy spectrum and adiabatic dynamics of vortex-core Majorana braiding and provide theoretical guidance for designing robust braiding protocols in realistic topological superconducting platforms.

AI.tldr: Time-dependent many-body simulations show nonmagnetic impurity effects on vortex-core Majorana braiding depend on impurity sign and gate type: attractive impurities can degrade \(\sqrt{Z}\)-gate geometric-phase quantization by suppressing the topological gap, while four-MZM \(X\)-gate success is mainly sensitive to braiding speed and specific impurity configurations.
AI.motivation: Vortex-core Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in topological superconductors are a leading platform for braiding-based quantum gates, but realistic devices contain nonmagnetic impurities whose impact on low-energy spectra and adiabatic braiding dynamics is not well understood.
AI.method: Time-dependent many-body simulations of vortex-core Majorana braiding in two configurations: a two-MZM \(\sqrt{Z}\) gate and a four-MZM \(X\) gate, comparing attractive versus repulsive nonmagnetic impurities, with diagnostics including the topological gap \(\Delta_t\), adiabaticity, geometric-phase-difference quantization, zero-energy nonequilibrium LDOS, low-energy spectra, and gate success probability; mitigation via slower braiding or a \(2a_0\) detour is tested.
AI.result: In the two-MZM \(\sqrt{Z}\) gate, sufficiently strong attractive impurities suppress \(\Delta_t\), reduce adiabaticity, and degrade geometric-phase-difference quantization; repulsive impurities cause no comparable damage despite stronger zero-energy nonequilibrium LDOS distortions. Slowing the braid or a \(2a_0\) detour restores near-quantization. In the four-MZM configuration, attractive impurities leave the low-energy spectrum nearly unchanged, while repulsive impurities mainly suppress the first excited state; slower braiding substantially improves \(X\)-gate success, and a specific attractive-impurity pair yields near-unit success (\(\approx 0.9985\)), unlike two weak repulsive impurities.
AI.conclusion: Nonmagnetic impurities affect vortex-core Majorana braiding in a sign- and gate-dependent manner, and robust braiding can be recovered through slower braiding or geometric detours; these results offer theoretical guidance for designing resilient braiding protocols in realistic topological superconducting platforms.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
comment: 5 main pages, 2 main figures. 15 total pages. Accepted in NeurIPS 2026 EvoRobust Workshop
summary: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

AI.tldr: The authors encode published belief-propagation decoders for quantum LDPC codes in a domain-specific language and use grammatical evolution to search it, yielding decoders faster and more accurate than tuned baselines (e.g., BP+OSD-0).
AI.motivation: Quantum error-correction decoding must remove noise reliably and fast enough to keep up with continuous measurement. Existing hand-designed BP decoders (BP+OSD, BP+LSD) are opaque in their parameterisation and leave performance headroom unexplored; the authors want an intermediate representation that preserves expert intuition while enabling automated optimization.
AI.method: Published BP decoders for qLDPC codes are re-implemented in a DSL, which exposes their parameters explicitly. This allows re-parameterisation of BP+OSD and BP+LSD with damping prior to search. Grammatical evolution then searches the DSL space to discover new decoder programs.
AI.result: Re-parameterised damped decoders are 17.1--41.0x faster at higher error rates, with BP+OSD-0 about 103x faster than the tuned ldpc-package version on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. An evolved decoder achieves 23% fewer logical errors than damped BP+OSD-0 at 0.64x its time; random-code-evolved decoders beat tuned BP+OSD-0 at <=1/31 of its time. The two fastest evolved decoders, frozen at one operating point, generalize across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, remaining on the time-error front.
AI.conclusion: Embedding expert knowledge in a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer bridging human intuition and machine-driven optimization, enabling highly efficient quantum error correction.

title: High-fidelity control of long-lived data qubits via a noisy mediator
summary: Long-lived qubits are attractive for storing quantum information, but they are often difficult to control or couple directly. A common strategy is to use mediator qubits to generate effective interactions for gate implementation. However, the mediator typically has a shorter coherence time than the data qubits, so mediator relaxation and dephasing are expected to limit the achievable gate fidelity. Here, we show that this limitation can be overcome. We present a reset-assisted control method that suppresses mediator-induced errors and enables high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on a quantum register of long-lived data qubits. Although mediator quantum jumps render the data-qubit evolution stochastic, repeated mediator reinitialization drives the resulting evolution paths toward the desired target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory analysis reveals the physical mechanism of error suppression and provides compact fidelity formulas for adapting the method to different platforms. Our results relax the requirement for long mediator coherence, broadening the range of mediators that can support high-fidelity control.

AI.tldr: A reset-assisted control scheme suppresses mediator-induced errors, enabling high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates on long-lived data qubits despite poor mediator coherence.
AI.motivation: Long-lived data qubits are hard to control or couple directly, so mediator qubits are used; but mediators typically have shorter coherence times, and their relaxation/dephasing is expected to limit gate fidelity.
AI.method: Repeated reinitialization (reset) of the mediator qubit. Although mediator quantum jumps make data-qubit evolution stochastic, repeated reinitialization drives the evolution paths toward the target operation. An analytical quantum-trajectory analysis explains the error-suppression mechanism and yields compact fidelity formulas for adapting the method to different platforms.
AI.result: The coherence limitation is overcome: high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates are achieved on a register of long-lived data qubits, with analytical fidelity formulas quantifying performance.
AI.conclusion: The requirement for long mediator coherence is relaxed, broadening the range of mediators that can support high-fidelity quantum control.

title: A New Quantum Algorithm Framework for Integer Order Entropy Estimation
summary: Entropy estimation for unknown distributions is a basic problem in statistical property estimation. In this paper, we propose a quantum algorithm framework for estimating Rényi entropy with fixed integer order $k\geq 2$. Given purified quantum query-access to a distribution on $n$ symbols, our algorithm estimates its order-$k$ Rényi entropy to within additive error $ε$ using $$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{n^{u_k}}{ε^{1-u_k}} + \frac{n^{(k-1)/(2k)}}ε\right)$$ queries, where $u_k=\max_{2\leq j\leq k} \frac{(3k-j)2^{j-2}-k}{k(2^j-1)}$. The main ingredient is a recursive construction of collision states in which intermediate states are retained and reused. We bound both the preparation and reflection costs, and choose the number of retained states at each order so that all recursive steps fit within a common query budget. We combine this construction with a sequence of decreasing probability thresholds, estimating the contribution of the labels found along the way separately from the remaining power sum. A batch estimator gives the required bound in the high-precision regime, and an initial search removes the need for prior knowledge of the power sum.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum algorithm framework for estimating Rényi entropy of fixed integer order k ≥ 2 for unknown distributions with purified quantum query access, achieving additive error ε with a query complexity of Õ(n^{u_k}/ε^{1-u_k} + n^{(k-1)/(2k)}ε), where u_k = max_{2≤j≤k} ((3k-j)2^{j-2} - k)/(k(2^j - 1)).
AI.motivation: Entropy estimation for unknown distributions is a fundamental problem in statistical property estimation, and quantum algorithmic approaches can potentially offer query-complexity advantages over classical methods for estimating Rényi entropy of order k ≥ 2.
AI.method: The core ingredient is a recursive construction of collision states in which intermediate states are retained and reused; the authors bound both preparation and reflection costs and tune the number of retained states at each order so that all recursive steps fit within a shared query budget. This is combined with a sequence of decreasing probability thresholds, separately estimating the contribution of labels found along the way versus the remaining power sum. A batch estimator handles the high-precision regime, and an initial search eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the power sum.
AI.result: The algorithm estimates the order-k Rényi entropy of a distribution on n symbols to within additive error ε using Õ(n^{u_k}/ε^{1-u_k} + n^{(k-1)/(2k)}ε) queries, with u_k as defined above.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a recursive, resource-reuse quantum framework for Rényi entropy estimation whose query complexity is characterized explicitly and improves scalability by avoiding assumptions about prior knowledge of the power sum.

title: Flat bands and bound states in the continuum in non-Hermitian pseudospin lattices
summary: Flat bands support compact localized states (CLSs), whereas bound states in the continuum (BICs) remain spatially localized despite having energies embedded in the continuum of extended states. Here, we investigate the connection between these phenomena in a class of one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices whose Bloch Hamiltonians take the pseudospin form H(k)=d(k)S. For integer pseudospin, the Hamiltonian intrinsically supports a zero-energy flat band and its associated compact localized states. When the effective pseudospin field has real transverse components and a purely imaginary longitudinal component, increasing non-Hermiticity compresses the dispersive bands toward the intrinsic zero-energy flat band, enabling their spectral overlap within a finite parameter range. The CLSs thus become embedded in the dispersive continuum and emerge as BICs. Adding a momentum-dependent Hermitian component along the gain-loss direction generally removes this spectral overlap without destroying the CLSs. We further extend this spectral mechanism to integer-pseudospin-n systems. These findings establish a connection between intrinsic flat-band localization and BIC formation through non-Hermitian spectral reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Integer-pseudospin non-Hermitian lattices with H(k)=d(k)·S intrinsically host a zero-energy flat band with compact localized states; strong non-Hermiticity compresses dispersive bands to overlap it, turning CLSs into bound states in the continuum.
AI.motivation: Flat-band compact localized states and bound states in the continuum are both localization phenomena, but whether and how they are connected is unclear. The paper aims to establish a link between intrinsic flat-band localization and BIC formation.
AI.method: Studies one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices whose Bloch Hamiltonians take the pseudospin form H(k)=d(k)·S with integer pseudospin, giving an intrinsic zero-energy flat band and CLSs. Considers an effective pseudospin field with real transverse components and purely imaginary longitudinal component, and tunes non-Hermiticity to drive spectral overlap of dispersive bands with the flat band; also adds a momentum-dependent Hermitian term along the gain-loss direction, and generalizes to integer-pseudospin-n systems.
AI.result: Increasing non-Hermiticity compresses the dispersive bands toward the intrinsic zero-energy flat band, producing spectral overlap over a finite parameter range, so the CLSs become embedded in the dispersive continuum and appear as BICs. A momentum-dependent Hermitian component along the gain-loss direction generally removes the overlap while preserving the CLSs. The mechanism extends to integer-pseudospin-n systems.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermitian spectral reconstruction connects intrinsic flat-band localization to BIC formation, offering a design principle for embedding localized flat-band states in a continuum.

title: The influence of quantum scarring on the onset of Bohmian chaos
summary: In the present work we investigate how the stable and unstable periodic orbits of a perturbed two-dimensional oscillator influence the Bohmian trajectories of the corresponding quantum system. In particular, we find that in our systems all Bohmian trajectories become chaotic in the long run and examine the times needed for them to approach their ergodic pattern. We show that these times are systematically shorter for orbits close to unstable periodic orbits than for orbits close to stable periodic orbits of the same period. We demonstrate that this behaviour is connected to scarring effects associated with both unstable and stable periodic orbits. We also investigate how the Bohmian dynamics changes when a stable periodic orbit undergoes a bifurcation and becomes unstable.

AI.tldr: Bohmian trajectories in a perturbed 2D oscillator all become chaotic long-term; the ergodic-approach time is systematically shorter for orbits near unstable periodic orbits than near stable ones, a behavior tied to scarring associated with both types of periodic orbits, including through a bifurcation.
AI.motivation: To understand how the stable and unstable periodic orbits of a classically perturbed two-dimensional oscillator govern the Bohmian trajectories of the corresponding quantum system, and in particular how classical orbit stability is imprinted on quantum (Bohmian) dynamics.
AI.method: Bohmian (de Broglie–Bohm) trajectory analysis of a perturbed 2D oscillator: comparing Bohmian trajectories launched near stable versus unstable periodic orbits of the same period, measuring the times required to reach their ergodic (chaotic) pattern, and linking these times to quantum scarring by the periodic orbits; additionally tracking the Bohmian dynamics across a bifurcation where a stable periodic orbit becomes unstable.
AI.result: All Bohmian trajectories become chaotic in the long run; the times to approach the ergodic pattern are systematically shorter for orbits close to unstable periodic orbits than for those close to stable periodic orbits of equal period; this behavior is connected to scarring effects associated with both unstable and stable periodic orbits.
AI.conclusion: Classical orbital stability of periodic orbits qualitatively and quantitatively controls Bohmian chaos onset — unstable orbits yield faster ergodization than stable ones via scarring — and the Bohmian picture changes accordingly when a stable orbit bifurcates into an unstable one.

title: Finite-Key Analysis for Multiple-Antenna Quantum Key Distribution with Continuous Variables
comment: The paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications (JSAC)
summary: Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) techniques, known for their use in wireless communications, can also find applications in quantum communications systems. This is, for instance, relevant to satellite-based quantum communications when atmospheric turbulence and the time-varying nature of the channel can make their implementation difficult. Here, we study the application of MIMO techniques to continuous-variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) in the realistic setting where a finite number of signals are exchanged. We show how data collected during the brief overpass time of low-earth-orbit satellites over ground stations can be processed to estimate MIMO channel parameters, extract a secret key, and quantify the key generation rate. For $2\times 2$ MIMO settings with Gaussian encoding and heterodyne detection, our finite-key analysis indicates that MIMO CV-QKD could outperform both multiplexed (with a nominal 3~dB improvement) and single-mode (with a nominal 6~dB nominal improvement) scenarios. Furthermore, we conjecture that the ultimate enhancement of a multiple-antenna CV-QKD system can be characterized by the product of the number of its inputs and outputs.

AI.tldr: Applies MIMO techniques to continuous-variable (CV) QKD over atmospheric satellite links with finite-key analysis, showing 2×2 MIMO—Gaussian encoding and heterodyne detection—improves key rates by ~3 dB over multiplexed and ~6 dB over single-mode scenarios, and conjecturing ultimate gain scales with the product of input and output antenna counts.
AI.motivation: Satellite-based CV-QKD suffers from atmospheric turbulence and time-varying channel conditions that degrade link performance; MIMO, proven in wireless communications, is proposed as a remedy, but its realistic finite-key performance for CV-QKD had not been established.
AI.method: Finite-key analysis of MIMO CV-QKD in a realistic low-earth-orbit satellite setting. Data collected during the brief ground-station overpass is processed to estimate MIMO channel parameters, extract a secret key, and quantify the key generation rate, for a 2×2 MIMO configuration with Gaussian modulation and heterodyne detection.
AI.result: Finite-key analysis indicates MIMO CV-QKD outperforms multiplexed scenarios by a nominal 3 dB and single-mode scenarios by a nominal 6 dB; a conjecture is proposed that the ultimate enhancement is characterized by the product of the number of inputs and outputs.
AI.conclusion: MIMO is a viable route to boost satellite-based CV-QKD under turbulence, with gains demonstrated under finite-key, realistic overpass constraints, and a scaling conjecture linking enhancement to the input-output antenna product.

title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
summary: Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "classical complexity" — the minimum classical communication cost of preparing quantum states — and shows it equals the classical communication needed to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, scaling exponentially with quantum dimension and as a power-law in inverse noise, with certification tools provided.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication naturally transmits quantum information, but it is unclear how difficult it is to reproduce such transmission using only classical communication resources. The authors seek a quantitative measure of the quantum advantage in communication.
AI.method: They introduce classical communication models for quantum preparations and define their minimum cost as the classical complexity. They prove a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments. They then characterise the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space and develop certification tools: an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations, and convex programming scalable to hundreds or thousands of qubit states.
AI.result: Classical complexity equals the classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments. For the noisy quantum state space it grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise, revealing rapidly scaling fundamental simulation cost.
AI.conclusion: Classical complexity is established as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, quantifying the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and offering practical, scalable certification tools.

title: Local-channel inequivalence within analytic symmetry-broken phases
summary: Gibbs states at different temperatures can be inequivalent under two-way quasi-local channels even within a single phase with spontaneously broken continuous symmetry and analytic free energy. We prove this for the symmetry-invariant Gibbs states of a canonical ideal Bose gas at fixed density and a classical vortex-free Villain model on hypercubic lattices in $d\ge3$ dimensions. At lower temperatures, two distant observers can estimate the shared direction of order more accurately. The maximum mutual information they can obtain by separate measurements grows logarithmically with the radius of their regions. The leading term is the same throughout each ordered phase, while the constant term $\mathcal{C}(T)=\tfrac12\ln[Υ(T)/T]+c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is strictly larger at lower temperatures. Here $Υ(T)$ is the phase stiffness and $c_{\mathrm{geom}}$ depends only on the region geometry. A quasi-local channel cannot increase this constant, so it is invariant under two-way conversion. Cooling would increase it and is therefore impossible between any two distinct temperatures in the ordered phase. On finite lattices, cooling with vanishing error requires a circuit whose causal radius grows at least linearly with the lattice side length. We also obtain the invariant for quantum and multicomponent Villain models and conjecture a stiffness formula for more general patterns of continuous symmetry breaking.

AI.tldr: Gibbs states at different temperatures within a single ordered phase of continuous-symmetry-breaking systems are shown to be inequivalent under two-way quasi-local channels by identifying a monotone invariant built from the constant term of the logarithmic growth of mutual information.
AI.motivation: Standard phase-equivalence notions (analytic free energy, same spontaneous symmetry breaking pattern, same phase) do not distinguish Gibbs states at different temperatures.
