The authors ask whether quasi-local convertibility provides a finer classification, and whether cooling within a single ordered phase is fundamentally impossible.
AI.method: They analyze symmetry-invariant Gibbs states of the canonical ideal Bose gas at fixed density and the classical vortex-free Villain model on hypercubic lattices in d≥3. Two distant observers measure their local regions to estimate the shared order direction; the maximum mutual information is computed asymptotically in the region radius. A constant term C(T)=½ln[Υ(T)/T]+c_geom is extracted, with Υ(T) the phase stiffness and c_geom a geometry-only factor. The behavior of this constant under two-way quasi-local channels is bounded. The construction is extended to quantum and multicomponent Villain models.
AI.result: The maximum mutual information obtainable by separate measurements grows logarithmically with region radius, with a leading coefficient identical throughout the ordered phase, while the constant term is strictly larger at lower temperatures. Since a quasi-local channel cannot increase this constant, it is invariant under two-way conversion. Consequently, cooling between any two distinct temperatures in the ordered phase is impossible. On finite lattices, cooling with vanishing error requires a circuit whose causal radius grows at least linearly with the lattice side length.
AI.conclusion: A stiffness-based mutual-information constant serves as a temperature-sensitive, channel-monotone invariant that separates Gibbs states across an entire ordered phase, establishing a no-go for cooling under quasi-local operations and a geometric lower bound on finite-lattice cooling circuits. A generalized stiffness formula is conjectured for broader continuous symmetry-breaking patterns.

title: A receiver-side approach to confirm phase randomization in BB84 time-bin QKD with weak coherent pulses
summary: In quantum cryptography using time-bin BB84 protocols, the relative phase of symbol pulses has to be random to avoid vulnerability to coherent attacks. Typically this phase randomization is checked on the sender side. Here, we propose a protocol for monitoring and confirming phase randomization independently on the receiver side during operation. The proposed method can be implemented on the single-photon level without the need for any physical adaptation of the receiver. This can provide an additional tool for monitoring against possible eavesdropping attempts that affect the phase randomization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a receiver-side protocol for monitoring and confirming that the relative phase of symbol pulses in time-bin BB84 quantum key distribution is properly randomized, operating at the single-photon level without requiring any physical modification of the receiver.
AI.motivation: In time-bin BB84 protocols, random relative phase between symbol pulses is required to prevent vulnerability to coherent attacks. This phase randomization is conventionally verified only on the sender side, leaving it unchecked during operation on the receiving end and thus open to eavesdropping strategies that manipulate randomization.
AI.method: A protocol enabling independent, receiver-side monitoring and confirmation of phase randomization during live operation. It is designed to work at the single-photon level and requires no physical adaptation of the existing receiver hardware.
AI.result: The method provides an additional monitoring capability that can detect possible eavesdropping attempts affecting the phase randomization, complementing sender-side checks without altering receiver implementation.
AI.conclusion: Receiver-side phase-randomization monitoring serves as a practical supplementary security tool for time-bin BB84 QKD systems, implementable on standard receivers at single-photon level.

title: Ellis: Extremely Fast Quantum Circuit Simulation under Qubit Loss and Leakage
summary: Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors: while a qubit remains lost or leaked, every operation acting on it is dropped. Consequently, the Clifford circuit executed differs from shot to shot. This variation breaks Pauli-frame simulation, which constructs each shot by XORing sampled Pauli flips onto a single \emph{common reference} measurement record. By rethinking the roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation, we show that many key fault-tolerant primitives nevertheless retain a common reference under loss. These include CSS code memory, lattice surgery, and transversal CNOT. Such circuits can therefore be simulated exactly under Pauli noise and loss by a Pauli frame with per-shot masks for the dropped operations. We define \emph{frame-CSS} circuits as those that are CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model that specifies where qubits can be lost and reloaded. We prove that every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference, and we give a practically near-linear-time procedure that certifies whether a circuit is frame-CSS. We implement the certifier and a high-performance simulator in the open-source package \href{https://github.com/isaachyw/ELLIS}{\textsc{Ellis}} (Efficient Loss and Leakage Invariant-reference Simulation). On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, \ellis{} samples 952{,}000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least $1000\times$ faster than Clifft~\cite{chase2026} and PPVM~\cite{luo2026ppvm}.

AI.tldr: The authors show that key fault-tolerant primitives (CSS memory, lattice surgery, transversal CNOT) retain a common reference under qubit loss/leakage, enabling exact Pauli-frame simulation with per-shot masks; they define frame-CSS circuits, prove they always have a common reference, give a near-linear-time certifier, and release ELLIS, which samples 952k shots/s on the gross code — ≥1000× faster than Clifft and PPVM.
AI.motivation: Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors that cause every operation on a lost/leaked qubit to be dropped, so the executed Clifford circuit varies shot to shot. This breaks standard Pauli-frame simulation, which XORs sampled Pauli flips onto a single common reference measurement record. The paper seeks a way to recover exact, fast simulation for important fault-tolerant circuits despite this per-shot circuit variation.
AI.method: The authors rethink the roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation. They identify that many fault-tolerant primitives retain a common measurement reference under loss, and formalize frame-CSS circuits (CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model specifying loss/reload locations). They prove every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference and design a practically near-linear-time certifier for frame-CSS. Simulation is done exactly under Pauli noise and loss via a Pauli frame with per-shot masks for dropped operations. The certifier and simulator are implemented in the open-source ELLIS package.
AI.result: On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, ELLIS achieves 952,000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least 1000× faster than Clifft and PPVM.
AI.conclusion: Frame-CSS circuits admit a common reference, making exact Pauli-frame simulation possible even with loss/leakage-driven per-shot circuit variation; this covers major FT primitives and yields a highly efficient, certifiable simulation framework (ELLIS).

title: The role of complementarity and quantum correlation in the uncertainty relations and the optimum states
summary: Uncertainty relations are used in quantum mechanics to illustrate the complementarity of two observables, assuming there is a lower bound for the product of their dispersions that depends on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation of those observables in an optimum state. In this work, we demonstrate that the complex parameter of the optimum state equation has real and imaginary parts that depend on the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation between the observables in the optimum state, respectively. We apply our results to a two-level system, finding that the first-order quantum correlation and the commutation relation of two spin-1/2 projections in the optimum state complement each other and, finally, when the term correlation is used, a lower bound for the uncertainty principle does not depend on any parameter of the optimum state, in contrast to the usual form of the Heisenberg principle.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes the complex parameter of the optimum-state equation underlying quantum uncertainty relations into real and imaginary parts, showing they are governed by the first-order quantum correlation and the commutator of the observables, respectively, and applies this to a two-level (spin-1/2) system.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty relations typically bound the product of dispersions via a lower limit depending on the first-order quantum correlation and the observable commutator evaluated in an optimum state. The authors seek to clarify the internal structure of the optimum-state equation's complex parameter and how correlation and commutation each contribute to the uncertainty bound.
AI.method: They analyze the complex parameter entering the optimum-state equation and demonstrate analytically that its real part is determined by the first-order quantum correlation while its imaginary part is determined by the commutation relation between the observables in the optimum state. The framework is then applied to a two-level system, examining two spin-1/2 projections.
AI.result: For the two-level system, the first-order quantum correlation and the commutator of the two spin-1/2 projections in the optimum state are shown to be complementary. Moreover, when the correlation term is used, the lower bound of the uncertainty principle becomes independent of any parameter of the optimum state, unlike the conventional Heisenberg form.
AI.conclusion: The complex optimum-state parameter cleanly separates correlation (real part) and commutation (imaginary part) contributions. This yields a state-parameter-independent lower bound for the uncertainty relation in the spin-1/2 case, offering a refined complementarity picture relative to the standard Heisenberg formulation.

title: Improving the signal-to-noise ratio through postselection of coincident detections in anticounterfeiting and quantum key distribution
summary: In quantum communications and other photon-counting applications, reliably detecting weak optical signals against a strong noise background remains a fundamental challenge. In this paper, we develop a simple idea: when a signal is carried by pairs (or more generally multiplets) of photons emitted simultaneously, postselection of coincident detections recorded on two detectors makes it possible to improve-sometimes drastically-the Signal to Noise Ratio. Essentially, this is made possible by the fact that genuine and accidental coincidences scale differently with the width of the postselection window. As long as the window remains wide enough to retain detections from the same pair, the genuine coincidence rate is approximately unchanged. In contrast, coincidences formed from independent clicks decrease linearly as the window is narrowed. The resulting signal-to-noise ratio, therefore, increases inversely with the window width. Our approach makes it possible to reveal photon-pair signals that are otherwise hidden beneath a much stronger uncorrelated background. We analyze here applications of this idea to quantum key distribution, metrology, and anti-counterfeiting.

AI.tldr: Postselecting coincident clicks on two detectors within a narrow time window improves the signal-to-noise ratio when signals are carried by photon pairs, since genuine coincidences are roughly window-width independent while accidental ones scale linearly with it.
AI.motivation: Detecting weak optical signals against strong noise backgrounds is a fundamental challenge in quantum communications and photon-counting applications; photon-pair signals can be buried under much stronger uncorrelated background.
AI.method: Exploit that signals are carried by pairs (or multiplets) of simultaneously emitted photons; apply postselection of coincident detections on two detectors using a narrow time window. Genuine coincidences from the same pair remain approximately unchanged as long as the window retains both photons, whereas accidental coincidences from independent clicks decrease linearly with window width.
AI.result: The signal-to-noise ratio increases inversely with the postselection window width, enabling recovery of photon-pair signals otherwise hidden beneath a much stronger uncorrelated background; applications analyzed for quantum key distribution, metrology, and anti-counterfeiting.
AI.conclusion: A simple coincidence-postselection scheme can drastically improve SNR in photon-counting scenarios by exploiting the differing scaling of genuine versus accidental coincidences with window width, with promising uses in QKD, metrology, and anti-counterfeiting.

title: Cooperativity-enhanced single-photon emission in a topological quantum emitter chain
summary: Single-photon emitters are one of the key elements in state-of-the art quantum technologies, yet optimizing and manipulating their emission requires precise fabrication of the emitter systems themselves. Here, we propose a route to tailored single-photon emission by exploiting cooperative effects in a topological single-photon emitter chain. Although the involvement of multiple emitters normally suppresses single-photon emission, we show that localized topological edge modes restore single-photon emission and protect against local perturbations. At the same time, cooperative effects occur due to the collective nature of the edge modes, leading to directional emission and linewidth narrowing. Our findings open new possibilities for tailoring single-photon emission by combining cooperativity and topological effects.

AI.tldr: A topological chain of emitters uses localized edge modes to restore and protect single-photon emission despite multi-emitter suppression, while collective effects yield directional emission and linewidth narrowing.
AI.motivation: Single-photon emitters are central to quantum technologies, but optimizing and manipulating their emission requires precise fabrication of the emitter systems. The authors seek a route to tailored single-photon emission that exploits cooperative and topological effects rather than relying on fabrication precision.
AI.method: The authors propose a topological single-photon emitter chain and analyze its emission properties, examining how localized topological edge modes affect single-photon emission and robustness against local perturbations, and how the collective nature of these edge modes induces cooperative effects.
AI.result: Localized topological edge modes restore single-photon emission that would otherwise be suppressed by the involvement of multiple emitters, and they protect against local perturbations. Cooperative effects arising from the collective nature of the edge modes lead to directional emission and linewidth narrowing.
AI.conclusion: Combining cooperativity with topological effects offers new possibilities for tailoring single-photon emission, providing a fabrication-tolerant design principle for quantum photonic emitter systems.

title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
summary: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,μ$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,μ$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,μ$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

AI.tldr: In a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation, the effect of coherence on learning depends strongly on the task: richer observables improve prediction, coherence loss is not uniformly harmful, and chaotic forecasting alone degrades clearly at short T2.
AI.motivation: To clarify how dephasing and the choice of measured observables influence learning in a dissipative quantum reservoir, since prior intuitions about the benefits of coherence are task-agnostic and underexplored.
AI.method: Simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. Compared single- plus two-qubit observables against population-only readout at matched polynomial feature counts. Tasks: nonlinear autoregressive moving-average (NARMA) prediction, autonomous generation (readout trained with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation), chaotic forecasting, and a noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor. Performance benchmarked against a no-relaxation/no-dephasing reference across 10 reservoir realizations.
AI.result: Multi-observable readout outperforms population-only readout on NARMA. Most configurations exceed the coherence-free reference, most strongly at T2=1 μs (where total memory capacity drops) and still at T2=5–10 μs (where memory is merely redistributed across delays). Limit-cycle persistence shows no clear systematic dependence on coherence. Chaotic forecasting horizons at T2=1 μs shorten in all 10 realizations. On the strange non-chaotic attractor, the model yields a smooth, approximately closed orbit, capturing neither the target's scatter nor its pointwise trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence on learning is strongly task-dependent: dephasing can even improve some prediction tasks, while chaotic forecasting is consistently degraded, and complex attractor structure is not reproduced.

title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
summary: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

AI.tldr: CAVQS is a context-aware variational quantum circuit synthesis framework that combines QR-based unitary redistribution across overlapping blocks with ancilla-free dynamic (measurement/feedforward-aware) reconstruction of terminal blocks, substantially reducing two-qubit gate counts over QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN.
AI.motivation: Block-based variational synthesis reduces costly two-qubit gates but instantiates blocks independently, preventing simplification across block boundaries; additionally, fully unitary synthesis ignores opportunities from permitted output measurements and classical feedforward.
AI.method: Two components: (1) unitary redistribution via QR decomposition that transfers unitary factors between overlapping blocks while preserving the overall transformation and reshaping local targets to enable cross-block reductions; (2) dynamic reconstruction for blocks preceding permitted terminal measurements, using a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search plus analytic branch-unitary construction to build ancilla-free dynamic implementations minimizing expected CNOT cost.
AI.result: On random-circuit targets, mean two-qubit gate counts drop by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% versus QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN on common successful instances; on 4–6-qubit algorithm benchmarks, reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88% respectively.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting inter-block context (unitary redistribution) and measurement-permitted dynamicity (feedforward-aware reconstruction) yields consistent, substantial CNOT reductions over state-of-the-art variational synthesizers on both random and algorithm benchmarks.

title: A sensitivity-constrained polynomial method for DQC1 query complexity
summary: The polynomial method is one of the fundamental techniques for proving lower bounds on quantum query complexity, particularly in the BQP query model. In this work, we develop an analogue of the polynomial method for the DQC1 query model. We introduce the notion of {\em sensitivity approximate degree} for Boolean functions and show that it provides a lower bound on DQC1 query complexity. We establish several basic structural properties of this new measure. As a first result, we show that every nonconstant total Boolean function on $N$ input variables has sensitivity approximate degree $Ω(N)$, and hence requires $Ω(N)$ queries in the DQC1 model. Thus, unlike in the BQP query model, DQC1 admits no asymptotic query speedup for total Boolean functions. For symmetric partial Boolean functions, we give a complete characterization of the sensitivity approximate degree in terms of the separation between oppositely labeled Hamming weight layers. This yields a tight quadratic separation between sensitivity approximate degree and standard approximate degree, and also leads to tight quadratic separations between DQC1 and BQP query complexities. We further establish quantitative average-case classical simulation theorems for DQC1 algorithms. Finally, we apply our framework to Fourier analysis, obtaining a simple proof of an $Ω(N^{1/4})$ DQC1 query lower bound for the 2-Forrelation problem.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a polynomial-method analogue for the DQC1 query model via a new "sensitivity approximate degree" measure, proving DQC1 has no asymptotic query speedup for total Boolean functions and giving tight quadratic separations from BQP.
AI.motivation: The polynomial method is fundamental for BQP query lower bounds, but no analogous tool exists for the DQC1 (one-clean-qubit) model, leaving its query power poorly understood.
AI.method: Introduces the sensitivity approximate degree for Boolean functions as a lower-bound measure on DQC1 query complexity, establishes its structural properties, fully characterizes it for symmetric partial functions via separation of oppositely labeled Hamming weight layers, derives average-case classical simulation theorems, and applies it to Fourier analysis.
AI.result: Every nonconstant total Boolean function on N variables has sensitivity approximate degree Ω(N), so DQC1 requires Ω(N) queries; symmetric partial functions admit tight quadratic separations between sensitivity and standard approximate degree and between DQC1 and BQP; and an Ω(N^{1/4}) DQC1 lower bound for 2-Forrelation is obtained.
AI.conclusion: DQC1 admits no asymptotic query speedup for total Boolean functions (unlike BQP), yet can achieve quadratic query separations on partial functions, and the framework yields quantitative average-case classical simulations and simple Fourier-based lower bounds.

title: Adaptive Hamiltonian Identification via Quantum Reinforcement Learning under Non-Stationary Dynamics
summary: Accurate identification of the Hamiltonian governing a quantum system is important for quantum-system characterization, device calibration, simulation, and reliable operation of quantum hardware. In practical systems, however, the governing dynamics may vary over time because of parameter drift, changing control conditions, or transitions between operating regimes. In this work, we formulate Hamiltonian identification as a quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) problem in which a quantum agent processes sequential quantum-state observations and estimates the governing Hamiltonian parameters. We first consider stationary dynamics using a Vanilla-QRL agent and then introduce a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture to track non-stationary dynamics. The framework is evaluated on transverse-field Ising model systems under stationary dynamics, abrupt Hamiltonian switching, rapidly changing Hamiltonians, random switch locations over longer trajectories, and gradual Hamiltonian drift. We further compare the proposed approach with a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network (QGRNN) baseline and evaluate frozen policies on unseen trajectories. Results show that both approaches accurately reconstruct stationary Hamiltonians, while GRU-QRL provides substantially improved tracking under non-stationary dynamics. These results demonstrate the potential of recurrent QRL as an adaptive system-identification tool for monitoring time-varying quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates Hamiltonian identification as a quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) problem, using a quantum agent to estimate Hamiltonian parameters from sequential quantum-state observations, and introduces a recurrent GRU-QRL agent that robustly tracks time-varying (non-stationary) Hamiltonians better than a stationary-oriented baseline.
AI.motivation: Accurate Hamiltonian identification underpins quantum-system characterization, device calibration, simulation, and reliable hardware operation, but real systems exhibit time-varying dynamics due to parameter drift, changing control conditions, or regime transitions—challenging methods that assume stationary Hamiltonians.
AI.method: The task is cast as a QRL problem where a quantum agent processes sequential quantum-state observations and estimates governing Hamiltonian parameters. A Vanilla-QRL agent handles stationary dynamics, and a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture is added for non-stationary tracking. Evaluation uses transverse-field Ising model systems under stationary dynamics, abrupt switching, rapidly changing Hamiltonians, random switch locations over longer trajectories, and gradual drift; comparisons are made against a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network (QGRNN) baseline, including frozen policies on unseen trajectories.
AI.result: Both approaches accurately reconstruct stationary Hamiltonians, while GRU-QRL delivers substantially improved tracking under non-stationary dynamics compared with the QGRNN baseline.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent QRL shows promise as an adaptive system-identification tool for monitoring time-varying quantum systems, motivating its use for online characterization and calibration of quantum hardware.

title: Efficient calculation of the full Laguerre-Gaussian spectrum of entangled biphotons
summary: The spatial biphoton state generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enables applications in high-dimensional quantum information processing and is often described in Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes. However, calculating the full LG spectrum for arbitrary radial and orbital angular momentum (OAM) indices requires computationally demanding multidimensional integrations. We present a generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral without approximating the phase-matching function. The source geometry can be completely described by a few dimensionless parameters, which reduce to two parameters for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists. Our derived expressions for the full LG spectrum allow for computationally efficient and numerically stable evaluation at high mode orders, addressing a crucial obstacle in previous works. To illustrate our approach, we compare OAM spectra obtained by projection onto the lowest radial order and by radially insensitive detection, and investigate how high-dimensional maximal entanglement can be approached by tuning source parameters. Our results provide a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.

AI.tldr: A generating-function method analytically evaluates the full Laguerre-Gaussian spatial biphoton spectrum in SPDC without approximating the phase-matching function, enabling stable, efficient computation at high mode orders.
AI.motivation: The full LG spectrum of the SPDC biphoton state, central to high-dimensional quantum information, conventionally requires computationally demanding multidimensional integrations, and prior approaches struggle with numerical stability and efficiency at high radial and OAM indices.
AI.method: A generating-function approach that analytically performs the four-dimensional transverse spatial integral while retaining the exact phase-matching function; source geometry is captured by a few dimensionless parameters, reducible to two for wave-vector-degenerate photons with equal waists.
AI.result: Closed-form expressions for the full LG spectrum that are computationally efficient and numerically stable at high mode orders; illustrative comparison of OAM spectra from lowest-radial-order projection versus radially insensitive detection, and analysis of how tuning source parameters approaches high-dimensional maximal entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a new analytical tool for efficiently characterizing and engineering high-dimensional spatial entanglement in SPDC.

title: A Tensor-Algebraic No-Go Theorem for High-Dimensional Photonic Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger States Discovered with AlphaProof Nexus
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, Lean examples. Comments welcome
summary: Photonic GHZ states generated with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs. In this representation, conditioning on an event with one photon in every detector turns the output amplitudes into coherent sums over perfect matchings, and generating an \(N\)-photon \(D\)-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. Here, we prove that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even \(N\ge4\) when \(D\ge N\). The proof, discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using AlphaProof Nexus, constructs a weighted sum \(\mathcal F\) of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex. Summing over the colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an \((N-1)\times N\) matrix of effective edge weights. For the graph amplitudes \(ω\) and GHZ target \(Δ\), the row--column imbalance yields \(\mathcal F(ω)=0\) but \(\mathcal F(Δ)\neq0\), contradicting the required equality \(ω=Δ\). Finally, we give a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered mathematical proof.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even N ≥ 4 when D ≥ N, ruling out a graph-based route to N-photon D-dimensional GHZ states from probabilistic pair sources; the proof was found via AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean.
AI.motivation: Photonic GHZ states built from probabilistic pair sources admit a description as edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs, where conditioning on one photon per detector yields coherent sums over perfect matchings. In this framework, producing an N-photon D-dimensional GHZ state reduces to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. The open question is whether such graphs can exist at all under the relevant parameter regime.
AI.method: A complex-weighted linear functional F of amplitudes is constructed, whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex. Summing over colours at one fixed vertex reduces the condition to an (N−1)×N matrix of effective edge weights. Comparing the graph amplitude ω with the GHZ target Δ yields a row–column imbalance: F(ω)=0 while F(Δ)≠0, contradicting ω=Δ. The proof was discovered by AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using AlphaProof Nexus.
AI.result: No complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even N ≥ 4 when D ≥ N. The invariant F(ω)=0 versus F(Δ)≠0 establishes the impossibility for all such parameter values.
AI.conclusion: The impossibility theorem closes off the monochromatic-graph construction of high-dimensional photonic GHZ states in the regime D ≥ N, and the authors provide a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered, formally verified proof.

title: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise
summary: Decomposing Hamiltonians into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. One such way of doing so is the contextual subspace decomposition, which expresses the Hamiltonian with respect to non-contextual sets of Paulis. The conditions for contextuality rely on the anticommutation and commutation of Pauli operators; it is therefore natural to make an explicit connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. Theoretical work is centered around two theorems: in the first, we consider non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and show that they are free-fermion-disguised. In the second we write these Pauli non-contextual Hamiltonians in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, showing that they carry a Jordan--Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. These two central theorems are formalized in the proof assistant language Lean. We use this to describe the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians, and highlight their relation to the more general class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. We further develop a heuristic algorithm to find line-graph based free-fermion fragments and their connected components of molecular Hamiltonians. We benchmark our algorithms against non-contextual searches for encoded molecular Hamiltonians and find comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components. Our work has implications for what fragments to consider as useful for quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: Non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are shown to be free-fermion-disguised and to admit a Jordan–Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding, with these theorems formalized in Lean; a heuristic line-graph algorithm yields free-fermion fragments of molecular Hamiltonians with performance comparable to non-contextual searches.
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian decomposition into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. Contextual subspace decomposition expresses the Hamiltonian via non-contextual Pauli sets, where contextuality is defined through commutation/anticommutation—suggesting a natural link between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. The paper aims to make this connection explicit and to identify which fragments are useful for simulation.
AI.method: Two central theorems: (1) non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are free-fermion-disguised; (2) they can be written in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, carrying a Jordan–Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. Both are formalized in the Lean proof assistant. The authors then characterize the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians and relate them to the broader free-fermion-disguised class. A heuristic algorithm is developed to find line-graph-based free-fermion fragments and their connected components in molecular Hamiltonians, benchmarked against non-contextual searches on encoded molecular Hamiltonians.
AI.result: Non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are proven free-fermion-disguised and shown to admit a Jordan–Wigner-like encoding (machine-checked in Lean). The space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians is described and positioned relative to general free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. The line-graph heuristic achieves performance comparable to non-contextual searches in identifying free-fermion-solvable components of encoded molecular Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: Non-contextuality in Pauli Hamiltonians is tightly linked to free-fermion structure, giving formal, verifiable characterizations and a practical fragment-finding heuristic. These results inform which Hamiltonian fragments should be considered useful for quantum simulation.

title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
summary: Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

AI.tldr: Introduces the "code quilt," a subsystem-code-based construction that directly measures joint logical Pauli-product operators between quantum code blocks without an ancillary system, with circuit-level and empirical analysis on bivariate bicycle and surface codes.
AI.motivation: Many proposals require fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements across code blocks beyond the surface code, but existing approaches (e.g., lattice surgery) typically need ancillary systems and extra physical qubits. The authors seek a construction that measures target joint logical operators directly, using only the ancillas already present for idle syndrome extraction.
AI.method: The code quilt is defined via a subsystem code whose gauge and stabilizer structure captures the joint logical operator across two or more code blocks. Explicit logical-measurement circuits are given that add no physical qubits beyond existing syndrome-extraction ancillas. The authors perform a structural analysis of the subsystem code and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the relevant code-capacity distance. Two protocol variants are presented: (i) direct measurement of gauge generators—provably not fault tolerant at large distance but practical, increasing physical qubit degree by at most two; (ii) a variant with better asymptotic properties, though general fault tolerance is unproven. An extensive empirical study applies the technique to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, searching for distance-preserving quilts over 25,000 random logical operators, optimizing sparse/decongested detector bases, and running decoding experiments.
AI.result: Code-capacity-distance-preserving quilts are found for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators on bivariate bicycle and surface codes. Sparse and decongested detector bases are optimized, and for a random subset, circuits estimated to be distance preserving are identified. Decoding experiments show logical error probabilities comparable to idle memory for the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and the distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between 1.5e-3 and 3e-3.
AI.conclusion: The code quilt offers an ancilla-free, low-overhead route to fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements across code blocks, with a practically implementable variant and strong empirical evidence of distance preservation and near-idle-memory logical error rates on representative bivariate bicycle and surface codes, though general fault tolerance of the asymptotically favorable variant remains an open problem.

title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
comment: 15 pages + 7 pages of appendices, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how much "irrealism" (distance of decoding observables from having elements of reality) is required to achieve given success probabilities in quantum random access codes, deriving exact irrealism frontiers for prepare-and-measure and entanglement-assisted codes.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how far decoding observables must be from possessing elements of reality to enable a target quantum advantage in a communication task; the paper addresses this for quantum random access codes by defining irrealism as the relative entropy to the closest undisturbed-preparation state.
AI.method: Defines irrealism as relative entropy relative to the closest preparation left undisturbed by the unrevealed measurement, capturing local coherence and correlations destroyed by that measurement, applicable to both PM and EA codes. Derives irrealism frontiers (least total irrealism per success probability) for PM codes with mutually unbiased bases, an excess-irrealism identity via Gibbs states of the decoding operator, minimization over decoders, and analysis of EA codes with qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent settings.
AI.result: For PM codes in mutually unbiased bases, the exact irrealism frontier is obtained in every dimension, with Gibbs states of the decoding operator uniquely attaining it. When minimized over decoders, required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not cheapest below success probability 0.833. For EA codes the frontier exceeds the PM frontier by the realism-based nonlocality of optimal-code contexts, and rank-one projective sender measurements certify a minimum realism-based nonlocality above success probability 0.815.
AI.conclusion: Irrealism provides a unified resource measure for quantum advantage in random access codes: it yields exact, dimension-general frontiers for PM codes and links EA-code advantage to realism-based nonlocality, enabling certification of shared-state nonlocality from observed success probabilities.

title: Entanglement, records, and quantum recovery in qubit chains
summary: We investigate entanglement, readable records and quantum recovery using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits. For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record is encoded in an off-diagonal element of the reduced density matrix and can be detected by a Pauli measurement, while a population measurement gives a higher-order signal. We further characterize the accessibility of the relative phase through joint transverse correlations and derive the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system and an accessible environment fragment. We show that interactions acting only within the environment can redistribute readable records and change the region required for quantum recovery without affecting the reduced state of the system.

AI.tldr: Using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits, the authors show that under weak interactions entanglement propagates to an environment site before an equally strong local record forms there, that the leading local record lives in an off-diagonal reduced-density-matrix element detectable by Pauli (not population) measurement, and that environment-internal interactions can redistribute readable records and change the fragment needed for quantum recovery while leaving the system's reduced state unchanged.
AI.motivation: The paper examines the relationship between entanglement, the emergence of readable (accessible) records in an environment, and the recoverability of quantum information, aiming to clarify how information about a system becomes locally accessible versus merely delocalized and how environment dynamics affect recovery regions.
AI.method: An exactly solvable model of sequentially interacting qubits is analyzed, distinguishing entanglement spreading from local-record formation via reduced density matrix elements, characterizing relative-phase accessibility through joint transverse correlations, and deriving the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system plus an accessible environment fragment.
AI.result: For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The dominant local record is off-diagonal in the reduced density matrix and is detected by a Pauli measurement, whereas a population measurement yields only a higher-order signal. Environment-internal interactions can redistribute readable records and alter the environment region required for quantum recovery without affecting the system's reduced state.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement spreading, record readability, and quantum recoverability are distinct notions in open-system dynamics: readable records can lag entanglement, reside in off-diagonal coherences, and be redistributed by environment-only interactions, decoupling the recoverable fragment from the system's reduced state.

title: Quantum Zeno Effect with a Superposed Measurement Schedule in Relational Time
summary: Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global system state is stationary, we propose a quantum circuit that explores the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom. We place two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in a coherent superposition using a schedule qubit. We show that, for a fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements taken. Then we show that, for one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, predicting a result that complements the standard Zeno probability. We propose a circuit implementation with physical memory qubits and show that measuring the memory register's joint $X$-basis parity distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one. We give the gate count and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit implementation. The Page-Wootters picture motivates this protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, although the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation. This is consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through correlations between a clock and the rest of the system.

AI.tldr: By superposing two quantum Zeno measurement schedules on a schedule qubit, the authors predict that interference visibility depends only on schedule time offset (not measurement count), find a "reversed Zeno" outcome, and propose a superconducting-qubit circuit whose memory-register X-basis parity distinguishes coherent from classical/dephased schedules.
AI.motivation: The Page-Wootters construction treats time as a quantum clock reading with a globally stationary state; the authors aim to turn this idea into a testable circuit that reveals observable consequences of making measurement timing itself a quantum degree of freedom.
AI.method: Two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit are placed in a coherent superposition via an ancillary schedule qubit. The interference visibility is analyzed as a function of the time offset and number of intermediate measurements; a circuit is designed with physical memory qubits and analyzed for gate count and error budget in a superconducting-qubit implementation.
AI.result: For fixed drive strength, the visibility between the two schedules depends only on their time offset, not on the number of intermediate measurements. For one schedule-readout outcome the Zeno trend reverses, complementing the standard Zeno probability. Joint X-basis parity of the memory register distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one.
AI.conclusion: The Page-Wootters picture motivates the protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, but the predictions follow from standard circuit dynamics without requiring a relational-time interpretation—consistent with Page-Wootters recovering standard quantum dynamics via clock-system correlations.

title: Effect of coupling asymmetry on the spontaneous decay and entanglement of two atoms in a common cavity
summary: We investigate the dynamics and the spontaneous decay of two identical two-level atoms into the vacuum in a cavity at low temperature. We analytically derive the survival probability and the amplitudes of the state of the system by calculating the exact self-energy when the atoms are both initially excited. It is found that moderate asymmetry enhances the decay of the survival probability and increases the entanglement production in either lossless and lossy cavities.

AI.tldr: In a low-temperature cavity, moderate asymmetry between two identical excited two-level atoms enhances their spontaneous-decay-driven survival-probability decay and boosts entanglement generation, both with and without cavity losses.
AI.motivation: To understand how asymmetry (e.g., differing atom-cavity coupling or positioning) affects the collective spontaneous decay and entanglement dynamics of two identical two-level atoms coupled to a low-temperature cavity vacuum.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of the survival probability and state amplitudes via an exact self-energy calculation for the case where both atoms are initially excited.
AI.result: Moderate asymmetry accelerates the decay of the survival probability and increases entanglement production, in both lossless and lossy cavities.
AI.conclusion: A moderate degree of asymmetry is beneficial, enhancing both the collective decay dynamics and entanglement generation of the atomic pair in a cavity vacuum environment.

title: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions
summary: Estimating the ground energy of interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum algorithms provide polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families. Classical approaches commonly rely on quantum Monte Carlo, where the sign problem is a major obstacle. However, even when a nonnegative expansion without sign problem is available, rigorous guarantees for rapid mixing are still far from well understood. In this paper, we give an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, which includes the attractive Hubbard models. This guarantee not only holds without a physical spectral gap or a weak-coupling assumption, but also covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. Technically, we first reduce ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and then use a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli and then apply the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. In addition, we obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling how many independent sampling runs and matrix updates are needed, and using sparse matrices to reduce the cost of each update.

AI.tldr: An efficient classical randomized algorithm approximates the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions (including attractive Hubbard models) via partition-function estimation, discretization to a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli, and the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem—without requiring a spectral gap or weak-coupling assumption.
AI.motivation: Ground-energy estimation for interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics. Quantum algorithms give polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families, while classical quantum Monte Carlo suffers from the sign problem. Even when a nonnegative (sign-problem-free) expansion exists, rigorous rapid-mixing guarantees remain poorly understood. This work aims to fill that gap with rigorous classical guarantees.
AI.method: The ground-energy estimation is reduced to partition-function estimation. A controlled-energy-error discretization yields a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli, to which the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem is applied. A sharper arithmetic bound is obtained by controlling the number of independent sampling runs and matrix updates, with sparse matrices reducing per-update cost.
AI.result: An efficient classical randomized algorithm is obtained that approximates the ground energy for conjugate hopping matrices with conjugate-paired orbital interactions, covering attractive Hubbard models and interactions beyond onsite density attraction. The guarantee holds without a physical spectral gap or weak-coupling assumption, and a sharper arithmetic bound is derived.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous classical polynomial-time guarantees for ground-energy estimation are established for sign-problem-free fermionic Hamiltonians beyond the onsite-attraction regime, linking partition-function estimation, discretization, log-concave counting, and sparse-matrix optimization into an efficient sampling scheme.

title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
summary: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces non-binary detector error models (DEMs) for circuit-level quantum error correction, modeling each faulty circuit location as one non-binary random variable instead of decomposing into independent binary mechanisms, and shows improved graph compactness and BP decoding performance.
AI.motivation: Standard DEMs in Stim and related work are binary: every non-binary circuit fault (e.g., a CNOT gate) is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. This decomposition is exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts, and it inflates the Tanner graph. The authors seek a representation that captures any Pauli channel exactly while yielding more compact graphs beneficial for hardware and decoding.
AI.method: They define non-binary DEMs where each fault location is a single random variable over its original alphabet (e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT). A split-merge-regroup transformation builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging error components that flip the same detectors and observables. They analyze equivalence of binary and non-binary DEMs under degenerate quantum MAP decoding, and use belief propagation (BP) which still passes a single scalar message per edge, with and without OSD post-processing.
AI.result: Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly (binary DEMs only for factorizing channels). When channels factorize, binary and non-binary DEMs are proven equivalent under degenerate quantum MAP decoding, but not under (non-degenerate) quantum MAP decoding. Numerically, on surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes, Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, and BP (with and without OSD) performs better than binary counterparts, with BP+OSD running up to 9.4x faster on CPU.
AI.conclusion: Non-binary DEMs give an exact, compact representation of circuit-level noise and lead to sparser Tanner graphs and faster, more accurate BP/OSD decoding, offering advantages for both hardware implementation and practical decoding of surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes.

title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
summary: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

AI.tldr: Entanglement-swapping's ideal functionality is unrealizable because a node that misreports classical outcomes gains influence over the delivered state; the authors propose a cut-and-choose protocol that certifies misreport rates above a minimum noise level while leaving untested pairs usable, quantifying test-pair and memory costs.
AI.motivation: Quantum repeaters need entanglement swapping to distribute entanglement over long distances, so its security matters. In a noisy network, intermediate nodes may perform operations faithfully yet misreport the classical outcome end users depend on, and existing verification approaches either cannot distinguish misreporting from readout noise or consume the states they certify.
AI.method: The authors prove the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realized (it grants the adversary no influence over the delivered state, unlike a relabeling node), showing that adding honest noise to the ideal setting does not help unless a bounded fraction of misreported pairs is conceded. They then design a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the remaining ones, with a finite-size guarantee and block-wise verify-and-release to bound memory.
AI.result: The protocol certifies errors above a pre-agreed minimum noise level (the misreport rate under the threat model), yielding a quality-of-service guarantee where failure witnesses non-delivery. Certifying 1% misreport on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs for minimum noise levels of 0–5%; the dominant cost is memory (10^5–10^6 pairs held at once). Block-wise release ties memory to block size at a weaker rate: a 10^4-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.
AI.conclusion: Ideal entanglement swapping is unrealizable under misreporting nodes, but cut-and-choose certification provides a practical quality-of-service guarantee, preserving untested pairs for use. Its main barrier is quantum memory rather than test overhead, and block-wise verification trades certification rate for feasible memory requirements.

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 Extended Data figures, 1 Extended Data table
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: Rapids is a streaming neural decoder co-designed with FPGA hardware that decodes surface-code syndromes in under a microsecond with far lower logical error rates than existing real-time decoders.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to keep pace with fast superconducting syndrome cycles. Existing decoders force a trade-off between speed and accuracy: fast decoders sacrifice accuracy, requiring larger codes and more physical qubits. A decoder that is both fast and accurate is therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors co-design a streaming neural decoder with an FPGA: the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and is trained in the FPGA's integer arithmetic, enabling efficient hardware realization.
AI.result: For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each syndrome round in under a microsecond on a single FPGA with low latency, achieving a logical error rate 240x lower than existing real-time hardware decoders. It extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, where it is 16x more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. The design also scales across multiple FPGAs or custom silicon.
AI.conclusion: Classical decoding hardware becomes an additional scalable resource, alongside qubits, that can be used to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
summary: Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that locally suppressing nuisance parameters is unnecessary in noisy quantum sensing; instead QEC must suppress Markovian noise locally while coherent control separates nuisance effects from the signal, yielding broadened Heisenberg-scaling regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing Markovian-dynamics error-correction approaches treat nuisance parameters and environmental noise alike by suppressing both locally, an assumption the authors argue is unnecessarily restrictive and obscures the fundamentally different constraints the two impose.
AI.method: A general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time-dependent Hamiltonian under both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise; derivation of a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, the exact optimal precision, and protocols that attain it, based on local QEC for noise plus optimally designed coherent control that separates accumulated nuisance effects from the target signal over the full evolution.
AI.result: Heisenberg scaling is attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance-parameter directions—in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise—substantially enlarging the attainable regime.
AI.conclusion: Markovian noise must be suppressed locally via QEC, but nuisance parameters need not (and generally should not) be eliminated locally; this distinction provides a general design principle for robust quantum sensors and a broader Heisenberg-scaling regime.

title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
summary: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.

AI.tldr: Decoding performance under disordered (space- and time-varying) noise is governed by a few information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: entropy sets the threshold, and Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold logical failure decay rate.
AI.motivation: Real quantum error correction experiments show heterogeneous, drifting noise, and characterizing it improves decoding, yet theory typically assumes fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. The authors aim to model decoding under incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels.
AI.method: Physical error rates are treated as random variables, and decoding performance is analyzed via information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution. Maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes are numerically studied across code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise, including distributions from open-access superconducting devices.
AI.result: The entropy of the noise distribution determines the threshold, while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Theory agrees well with numerics in all noise settings, and the framework yields a quantitative measure of the benefit of noise characterization.
AI.conclusion: For realistic error correction, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions may be more informative than reporting mean or median error rates of device components.

title: Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model
summary: Collective two-photon light--matter interactions enable pair amplification but can destroy spectral confinement, preventing a stable thermodynamic bright phase. We show that a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction renders the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of \(N\) emitters lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized \(\mathbb Z_4\) symmetry. We determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with \(O(N^{-1})\) finite-size control and obtain the global phase diagram. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization through \(N=128\) supports the predicted density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal--bright tunneling gap. Spectral collapse thus becomes the singular zero-Kerr point of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing pair amplification.

AI.tldr: Adding a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr term to the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian keeps it lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized Z4 symmetry, turning spectral collapse into a single singular point embedded in a first-order phase diagram.
AI.motivation: Collective two-photon light-matter interactions can amplify photon pairs but often destroy spectral confinement, so no stable thermodynamic bright phase exists. The authors seek a Hamiltonian route that cures spectral collapse while retaining the collective pair-amplification physics.
AI.method: Introduce a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction into the two-photon Dicke model of N emitters. Derive the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with O(N^{-1}) finite-size corrections, construct the global phase diagram, and corroborate with symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization up to N = 128.
AI.result: The Kerr term renders the Hamiltonian lower-bounded for all couplings and preserves the generalized Z4 symmetry. A bright minimum emerges at a saddle-node bifurcation and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, yielding a discontinuous photon-density jump. Numerics through N = 128 confirm the density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal-bright tunneling gap.
AI.conclusion: Spectral collapse is reinterpreted as the singular zero-Kerr limit of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a concrete Hamiltonian mechanism for stabilizing collective two-photon pair amplification.

title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
summary: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.

AI.tldr: This paper studies design choices for sequential entanglement generation with error detection over a repeater chain, using QKD as a benchmark, and finds that simple error-detecting codes—especially two-qubit repetition codes—perform well under near-term hardware and may suffice for many practical scenarios.
AI.motivation: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communication requires scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection offers manageable implementation requirements and a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure, but the key design choices for such schemes remain to be systematically investigated.
AI.method: The authors analyze design choices for sequential entanglement-generation schemes with error detection over a repeater chain, benchmarking performance with quantum key distribution. They compare simple quantum error-detecting codes (repetition codes, quantum parity codes) against unencoded strategies, examine alternative architectures for generating initial entanglement, and assess how hardware improvements trade off against one another.
AI.result: Simple quantum error-detecting codes—repetition codes or quantum parity codes—perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without encoding; two-qubit repetition codes may be all that is needed in many practical scenarios. Different initial-entanglement generation architectures show distinct merits, and moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate slow progress in others.
AI.conclusion: Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is an attractive near-term route to scalable quantum repeaters, and simple error-detecting codes such as two-qubit repetition codes offer a practical, low-overhead design choice, with hardware trade-offs providing partial resilience to uneven technological progress.

title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties.
