In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a QKD protocol that uses a party's physical position as the authentication credential, interleaving BB84 QKD with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds to achieve efficient authenticated key distribution.
AI.motivation: Standard QKD requires authentication so that parties do not unknowingly establish a key with an adversary impersonating an honest party. The authors motivate using physical position as the authentication credential and note that prior approaches were inefficient, requiring an entire QPV protocol per bit requiring authentication.
AI.method: The protocol consists of a BB84 QKD scheme with QPV rounds randomly interleaved, so that position serves as the authentication credential for key distribution. An initial security analysis is performed against a restricted set of attacks.
AI.result: The approach is efficient compared with previous schemes that required running a full QPV protocol for every bit needing authentication. Initial security analysis is given for a restricted attack set.
AI.conclusion: Position can serve as an efficient authentication credential for QKD by interleaving QPV rounds within an underlying BB84 protocol, though the security analysis is initial and limited to restricted attacks.

title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
summary:
Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026.
  Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$.
  Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof.
  Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise (CHN) problem, shows it lies in QMA but is hard for the QCMA hierarchy (QCMAH) in the query model, and uses it to construct a classical oracle separating QMA from QCMAH while collapsing P=BQP=QCMA=QCMAH, plus deriving quantum cryptographic primitives that survive even when P=QCMA.
AI.motivation: Motivated by Cakan's Codeword-Hash Structure problem (2026) aimed at separating QMA from QCIP, the work seeks to understand the power of quantum proofs (states) versus classical proofs, and to determine which quantum cryptographic primitives remain possible even under the collapse P=QCMA—where neither quantum one-way functions nor verifiable quantum advantage exist. It also addresses an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
AI.method: Defines a new problem, Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise (CHN), inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem, and proves in the query complexity model that CHN is in QMA yet hard for the QCMA hierarchy QCMAH = ∪_{d≥1} QCMA^{QCMA^{...}}. This hardness is leveraged via oracle-construction techniques to design a classical oracle O achieving P^O = BQP^O = QCMA^O = QCMAH^O ⊂ QMA^O while QMA^O ⊄ QCMAH^O, and to relativize quantum cryptographic primitives.
AI.result: Establishes a classical oracle O with P^O=BQP^O=QCMA^O=QCMAH^O ⊂ QMA^O but QMA^O ⊄ QCMAH^O, showing a quantum-state/proof advantage can persist even when classical computers solve every classically-verifiable quantum problem. Additionally, relative to such an oracle there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys/ciphertexts, among other primitives, despite the collapse P=BQP=QCMA=QCMAH.
AI.conclusion: Quantum proofs (states) confer strictly greater power than classical proofs relative to a classical oracle, and a broad class of quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when P=QCMA (with no quantum one-way functions or verifiable quantum advantage), answering Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal's open question.

title: Classically Trained Quantum Generative Models with Shared Training and Fine Tuning for Quantum Matter
summary: Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter. Selected correlations can guide the classical training of a quantum sampler even when sampling the full distribution is difficult. We ask whether training across related ground-state distributions helps the sampler reproduce their correlations more accurately. We train a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram before local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, we derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with a cost that depends on the circuit generators. We also introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. We study the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model, using an automated search to select reference calculations near phase transitions. On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4 by 256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits have lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than the independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry. These results motivate shared training for preparing quantum samplers across a phase diagram and local fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: A hypernetwork is trained to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across a phase diagram and then locally fine-tuning, so that quantum samplers reproduce ground-state correlations of the Haldane and transverse-field Ising models more accurately than independently fitted circuits.
AI.motivation: Sampling the full ground-state distribution is hard, but selected correlations can still guide classical training of a quantum sampler. The authors ask whether training jointly across related ground-state distributions (rather than fitting each point independently) helps the sampler reproduce correlations more accurately.
AI.method: A hypernetwork maps Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, pretrained across the phase diagram and then locally fine-tuned with additional reference data. For classical training they derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with cost depending on the circuit generators, and introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. Reference calculations are chosen near phase transitions via automated search; experiments cover the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model.
AI.result: On a twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4x256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits achieve lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry.
AI.conclusion: Shared training across a phase diagram followed by local fine-tuning is a promising route for preparing quantum samplers, motivating information-sharing pretraining as a practical strategy for deploying quantum circuits across parameter regimes.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
summary: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes end-to-end quantum algorithms for differential equations (classical input, classical output) and delivers a fully implemented one for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation with polylogarithmic circuit size and quasilinear-in-1/ε gate cost, showing exponential scaling improvement over classical methods.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum PDE algorithms rely on abstract oracle specifications and assumptions, leaving their practical feasibility and real computational advantage unclear. A concrete, fully implemented end-to-end algorithm is needed to assess practical quantum advantage.
AI.method: Defines end-to-end quantum PDE algorithms as accepting classical inputs and returning classical outputs, with implemented primitives from state preparation to property estimation. For the variable-coefficient LPB equation, the authors introduce a new discrete grid representation enabling an efficient operator oracle, and apply optimal wavelet preconditioning to obtain a solution cost independent of the discretized operator's condition number.
AI.result: Quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both grid points N_g and inverse accuracy 1/ε; overall gate cost polylogarithmic in N_g and quasilinear in 1/ε; classical preprocessing also polylogarithmic in N_g and 1/ε. Demonstrates exponential scaling improvement in N_g over classical methods.
AI.conclusion: Provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a practically valuable PDE, establishes its scaling advantages, and lays a foundation for evaluating practical quantum advantage.

title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
summary: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates for any $ε>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

AI.tldr: Novel in-place quantum arithmetic algorithms (modular multiplication, integer multiplication, modular inversion) achieving subquadratic gate counts (O(n^{1+ε})) with no or logarithmic ancilla qubits.
AI.motivation: Arithmetic operations are fundamental to quantum algorithms, and their implementation cost significantly affects the viability of quantum applications. Current state-of-the-art methods incur high space (ancilla) and gate-count overheads, motivating the need for more efficient in-place arithmetic.
AI.method: The authors derive a single unified theorem and use it to construct in-place algorithms for modular multiplication (modulo a power of two) with classical or quantum odd multiplier, standard in-place integer multiplication with non-zero classical or quantum multiplier, and in-place modular inversion (modulo a power of two), all achieving O(n^{1+ε}) gates.
AI.result: In-place modular multiplication, integer multiplication, and modular inversion all require O(n^{1+ε}) gates for any ε>0. The classical-multiplier cases use no ancilla qubits; the quantum-multiplier multiplication uses a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits. These are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for these in-place operations.
AI.conclusion: All but one of the fast operations are memory-optimal, requiring only space to store the output which overwrites the input. The unified theorem underlying the multiplication algorithms may find further application in quantum arithmetic.

title: Query-Optimal Quantum Minimum Finding from Numerical Estimators
summary: We propose a quantum minimum-finding algorithm for objectives accessed via numerical estimators that avoids the logarithmic query overhead of amplifying the confidence of estimates before the search. A coherent estimator that is $\varepsilon$-accurate with probability at least $2/3$ on each of $N$ labels suffices to find a $2\varepsilon$-optimal label using $O(\sqrt N)$ base-estimator queries at constant confidence. The query bound and the additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. More generally, suppose a preparation assigns probability mass at least a known $p$ to objective values at most $a$. Without knowing $a$ or the prepared distribution, our algorithm returns a candidate and an estimate $v$ such that, jointly with constant probability, $v$ is $\varepsilon$-accurate for the candidate and $v\le a+\varepsilon$. The algorithm uses $O(p^{-1/2})$ queries to each of the preparation and estimator oracles in the worst case, and the selected candidate can be retained as a quantum state. For preparation width $s_P$ and estimator workspace width $w$, it requires $O(s_P+w+\log\log(4/p))$ qubits, independently of the requested confidence. Applications give worst-case optimal $Θ(\sqrt N/η)$ queries for selecting an $η$-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation using $O(ω^{-1})$ preparations and $O((ωη)^{-1})$ elementary controlled-evolution queries at constant confidence, where $ω$ is a lower bound on the guiding state's ground-space amplitude overlap.

AI.tldr: A quantum minimum-finding algorithm works directly with numerical estimators, achieving worst-case-optimal O(√N) estimator queries at constant confidence without the log overhead of estimate amplification.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum minimum-finding must amplify each estimator's confidence before comparing values, incurring a logarithmic query overhead. The authors seek a search that operates on low-confidence coherent estimators directly, with worst-case-optimal query counts and additive error.
AI.method: Given a coherent estimator that is ε-accurate with probability ≥2/3 on each of N labels, the algorithm finds a 2ε-optimal label using O(√N) base-estimator queries at constant confidence. It is generalized to the setting where a preparation places probability mass ≥p on objective values ≤a (with a and the distribution unknown), returning a joint candidate plus estimate v with v ε-accurate for the candidate and v≤a+ε, using O(p^{-1/2}) queries to preparation and estimator oracles; candidate retained as a quantum state; qubit cost O(s_P+w+log log(4/p)), independent of confidence.
AI.result: The query bound and additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. Applications yield worst-case optimal Θ(√N/η) queries for selecting an η-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation using O(ω^{-1}) preparations and O((ωη)^{-1}) elementary controlled-evolution queries at constant confidence (ω a lower bound on ground-space amplitude overlap).
AI.conclusion: Avoiding pre-search confidence amplification removes logarithmic overhead while preserving worst-case optimality, giving a unified minimum-finding framework with state retention, low qubit cost independent of confidence, and improved guided ground-energy estimation.

title: High-temperature Gibbs states are uniformly Markovian and trivial
summary: We prove that, above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI). Specifically, we prove exponential decay of the CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ which need not comprise the entire system, thereby establishing a \textit{uniform Markov property} for high-temperature Gibbs states. A central obstruction to proving such bounds is that conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge due to noncommutativity. Our main insight is to construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state using an overcomplete basis. Although such representations generally involve negative quasiprobability weights, we show that a decomposition based on projective 2-designs admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperatures, allowing us to circumvent the obstruction. The separability of high-temperature Gibbs states is a natural byproduct of this decomposition. Finally, in the context of mixed-state phases of matter, our results imply that high-temperature Gibbs states belong to the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.

AI.tldr: Above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI), yielding a uniform Markov property for arbitrary spatial tripartitions; the key tool is a positive-weight cluster expansion built from a projective 2-design classical representation.
AI.motivation: Conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge because of noncommutativity, blocking proofs of information-theoretic correlation bounds (e.g., exponential CMI decay) for noncommuting local Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state in an overcomplete basis. Since such representations generally carry negative quasiprobability weights, the authors use a decomposition based on projective 2-designs, which is shown to admit a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperature.
AI.result: Exponential decay of mutual information and CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions A ⊔ B ⊔ C (not necessarily covering the whole system), establishing a uniform Markov property at high temperature. Separability of high-temperature Gibbs states follows as a byproduct, and these states are shown to lie in the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.
AI.conclusion: Noncommutativity obstructions can be circumvented via a positive-weight 2-design-based classical representation, giving a uniform Markov property and placing high-temperature Gibbs states in the trivial mixed-state phase.
